h1: How to Tell If Your Roof Has Hail Damage (Colorado Guide)
title: Hail Damage Roof Signs Colorado
description: How to tell if your roof has hail damage in Colorado: ground clues, shingle bruising, hail size chart, and what to photograph. Get a free inspection.
keywords: how to tell if roof has hail damage
excerpt: Hail damage on a Colorado roof is often invisible from the driveway and obvious up close. Here is how to read the ground clues, what real hail hits look like, and when to get an inspection.
intro:
The Front Range sits inside what meteorologists call Hail Alley, a band running from Wyoming through eastern Colorado and down into the Texas panhandle. Loveland, Fort Collins, Greeley, and Windsor average somewhere around seven to nine hail days a year, and the severe season runs from mid April to mid September. Colorado ranks second only to Texas for hail insurance claims, according to the Rocky Mountain Insurance Information Association, and the May 8, 2017 Denver metro storm remains the costliest insured catastrophe in state history at roughly $2.3 billion.

None of that tells you whether the storm that just rolled over your house hurt your roof. Hail damage is frequently invisible from the ground, and a roof that looks fine from the driveway can have dozens of bruised shingles per slope. This guide walks through what to look for at ground level, what real hail damage looks like on each roofing material, what to photograph, and when to call for an inspection before your claim window closes.

sections.h2: Start at ground level: the soft metal test
sections.html:
Before anyone gets on a ladder, walk the property and look at the soft metals. Aluminum, thin galvanized steel, and painted sheet metal dent at hail sizes well below what it takes to damage a shingle, so they act as a record of what fell. If the soft metals are clean, the roof is probably fine. If they are peppered, the roof needs a closer look.

  • Gutters and downspouts. Look along the top edge of the gutter and the face of the downspout for round dimples. Run your hand down the downspout and feel for dents you cannot see.
  • Air conditioner condenser fins. Hail flattens the thin aluminum fins on the side facing the storm. Crushed fins on one side and clean fins on the other tell you the direction of the storm.
  • Window screens and wraps. Torn or dimpled screens and dented aluminum window wraps are strong indicators.
  • Deck boards, fences, and painted wood. Fresh hail knocks bright chips out of stained or painted surfaces, exposing lighter wood underneath.
  • Vehicles, grills, mailboxes, and patio furniture. Any dented horizontal metal surface counts.
  • Granule piles. Check the splash blocks and the ground under each downspout. A fresh pile of black or colored granules that looks like coarse sand means the storm stripped the protective surface off your shingles.

Photograph everything you find, with a coin or tape measure for scale, and note the date and approximate time of the storm. These photographs matter later because they establish that hail of a damaging size fell on your property on a specific date.

sections.h2: What hail damage looks like on asphalt shingles
sections.html:
Hail damage on an asphalt shingle is a bruise, not a hole. The stone hits the shingle, crushes the granules into the asphalt layer, and fractures the fiberglass mat underneath. From a few feet away it looks like a dark spot about the size of the hailstone. Up close you can see the granules are gone and the black asphalt is exposed. Press the spot with your thumb and it feels soft or spongy compared to the shingle around it, the way a bruised apple feels under the skin.

Real hail damage has a few consistent traits:

  • Random pattern. Hits are scattered with no straight lines and no repeating spacing. Hail does not fall in rows.
  • Directional. The slopes facing the storm have more hits than the slopes facing away. A north facing slope with forty hits and a south facing slope with two is normal for a storm that came out of the northwest.
  • Round or slightly oval. Larger stones leave rounder marks. Wind driven hail leaves slightly oval marks, all elongated in the same direction.
  • Fresh exposure. New hits show shiny black asphalt. Old hits weather to a dull gray within a season or two.

Several things get mistaken for hail. Blistering from manufacturing defects or poor attic ventilation shows up as small raised bumps with granules popped off the top, usually scattered across every slope evenly. Foot traffic scuffs run in a line and follow the path a person would walk. Nail pops and thermal cracking follow the shingle layout. Ordinary granule loss from age is uniform and heaviest in the water channels. An inspector who has walked a lot of Colorado roofs can tell these apart quickly, and an adjuster will try to.

sections.h2: Metal, tile, cedar, and synthetic roofs
sections.html:
Different materials fail differently, and some of them hide damage better than shingles do.

Metal roofing. Standing seam and metal shingle panels dent rather than crack. Dents are cosmetic until the hail is large enough to crease the panel, split a seam, or fracture the paint film so corrosion can start. Many insurance policies now carry a cosmetic damage exclusion for metal roofs, which means dents alone may not be covered even when they are obvious. Look at the ridge cap, the exposed fasteners on trim, and any flat accessories like vent caps and pipe boots, which are often thinner gauge than the panels and dent first.

Concrete and clay tile. Tile cracks, chips at the edges, or breaks clean through. Chips are easy to see. Hairline cracks are not, and they let water onto the underlayment, which is what actually keeps a tile roof dry. Broken tile also tends to slide out of position over the following weeks. Our tile roofing inspections include lifting and checking tiles around the hit areas.

Cedar shake and shingle. Hail splits cedar along the grain, knocks out chunks at the butt edge, and leaves fresh light colored impact marks on weathered gray wood. Older cedar that is already cupped or split takes more damage from a given storm than new cedar.

Synthetic slate and shake. Most polymer products carry UL 2218 Class 4 ratings and shrug off hail up to 2 inches. Damage, when it occurs, shows up as cracks at the exposed edge or at the fastener line.

Flat roofs. Modified bitumen and TPO membranes bruise and puncture at seams, at the edges of insulation boards, and anywhere the membrane bridges a gap. Granulated cap sheets lose granules the same way shingles do.

sections.h2: Hail size and what it does to a roof
sections.html:
Most hail damage debates come down to size. The National Weather Service logs reports by comparison objects, and roofing inspectors use the same scale. These are typical thresholds, and they shift with wind speed, the age of the roof, and the angle of the slope.

Reported sizeDiameterTypical effect
Pea0.25 inchNo damage to roofing. Minor plant damage.
Dime to penny0.70 to 0.75 inchDents soft aluminum. Rarely damages shingles in good condition.
Quarter1.00 inchNWS severe threshold. Granule loss and bruising on older or standard shingles, especially with wind.
Half dollar1.25 inchBruising on most standard asphalt shingles. Dents thin metal accessories.
Golf ball1.75 inchFunctional damage to standard shingles, cracked tile, split cedar, dented metal panels.
Tennis ball to baseball2.5 to 2.75 inchPunctures standard shingles, breaks tile, dents and creases metal, can damage decking.
Softball4 inch and upDestroys most roofing. Holes in decking and skylights.

Class 4 impact rated shingles are tested with a 2 inch steel ball dropped from 20 feet under UL 2218, so a Class 4 roof in good condition often comes through a golf ball storm with cosmetic marks only. A fifteen year old standard shingle can show functional damage from quarter size hail driven by a 50 mph wind. The roof's age and condition matter as much as the stone.

Northern Colorado sees damaging hail most years. NWS storm reports for 2023 logged a record 796 reports of 1 inch or larger hail statewide, beating the prior record of 561 set in 2018. Loveland recorded golf ball hail on August 5, 2023, and the June 2018 storms dropped golf ball hail on Greeley and the foothills northwest of Fort Collins. If one of those cells crossed your neighborhood, assume your roof took hits until an inspection says otherwise.

sections.h2: What to photograph and record
sections.html:
Documentation is the difference between a smooth claim and an argument. Take these photographs within a day or two of the storm, before the evidence weathers.

  1. Wide shots of each side of the house, showing the roof slopes and the ground below them.
  2. Every dented soft metal item, with a coin, ruler, or tape in frame for scale.
  3. Granule piles under downspouts and in gutters.
  4. Hailstones themselves if any remain. Set them next to a ruler. Put a few in a freezer bag. Melted hail cannot be measured.
  5. Damage to vehicles, screens, and outdoor property, even if you do not plan to claim it. It proves the storm's intensity at your address.
  6. Interior ceilings below the roof, including closets and the attic if you can safely access it, to document that there was no leak before the storm and to catch any leak that develops afterward.

Write down the date, the time, how long the hail lasted, which direction the wind came from, and what size the stones looked like. Save any weather alerts on your phone. Later, an inspector or a claims professional can match your notes against NOAA storm reports and radar archives for your address.

Do not get on the roof yourself. Wet shingles and granule loss make a roof slick, and foot traffic on a freshly bruised roof can add damage that an adjuster will then attribute to you. A professional inspection is free and includes a photo report you keep whether or not you file a claim. If you have a leak you cannot wait on, our storm damage crews can tarp the roof the same day.

sections.h2: How inspectors and adjusters decide
sections.html:
Most carriers and most roofers use the same basic method. The inspector marks a 10 foot by 10 foot test square on each slope, counts the hail hits inside it, and notes the type of damage. A common rule of thumb in the industry is that eight or more functional hits in a test square qualifies the slope for replacement, though the threshold is set by the carrier and the policy, not by law. The inspector also checks the ridge, the valleys, the pipe boots, the vents, the flashing, the skylights, and the gutters, because those items are often damaged even when the field shingles are borderline.

There are a few ways a roof fails the test even with real damage on it. Hits that are counted as cosmetic rather than functional, hits on only one slope of a multi slope roof, and damage that the adjuster attributes to age, blistering, or mechanical causes all reduce what the carrier will pay. This is why the photographs from the soft metal walk around matter. A gutter with thirty dents the size of a half dollar is hard to argue with.

Timing matters as well. Most Colorado homeowner policies require prompt notice of a loss, and many set a contractual window, often one year from the date of loss, for wind and hail claims. Hail damage does not heal, but it does weather, and a bruise that is obvious in July is harder to prove in the following spring. If you think your roof took a storm, get it inspected while the evidence is fresh, read your policy for the notice deadline, and then decide whether to file. Our hail damage roof repair team will tell you plainly if the roof does not need a claim.

faq.q: Can hail damage a roof without any visible signs from the ground?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the normal case. A hail bruise on an asphalt shingle is about the size of the stone and dark against a dark roof, so it blends in from the driveway. Soft metals like gutters, air conditioner fins, and window screens show damage at smaller hail sizes than shingles do, which is why the ground level walk around is the first step. If the soft metals are dented, assume the roof needs an on roof inspection.

faq.q: How big does hail need to be to damage a shingle roof?
faq.a: There is no single number. Quarter size hail at 1 inch, which is the National Weather Service severe threshold, can bruise an older or standard three tab shingle when it is driven by wind. Golf ball hail at 1.75 inches usually causes functional damage to standard shingles. A Class 4 impact rated roof in good condition is tested to a 2 inch steel ball and often survives golf ball hail with cosmetic marks only.

faq.q: How long do I have to file a hail claim in Colorado?
faq.a: It depends on your policy, not on a statute. Policies require prompt notice of a loss, and many carriers set a contractual filing window, often one year from the date of the storm, for wind and hail damage. Read the conditions section of your policy or ask your agent. Getting a free inspection soon after a storm gives you a dated photo report so you can decide within the window.

faq.q: What is the difference between cosmetic and functional hail damage?
faq.a: Functional damage shortens the life of the roof or lets water in: a fractured shingle mat, a cracked tile, a split shake, a punctured membrane. Cosmetic damage changes the appearance without affecting performance, most often dents in metal panels. Carriers pay for functional damage. Many policies now exclude cosmetic damage, especially on metal roofs, so check your policy for a cosmetic damage exclusion endorsement before you file.

faq.q: Should I get on the roof to check for hail damage myself?
faq.a: No. Granule loss and wet shingles make a hailed roof slick, and walking on bruised shingles can add damage that an adjuster will attribute to foot traffic instead of the storm. Do the ground level walk around, photograph the soft metals and any granule piles, and schedule a professional inspection. Ours are free, photo documented, and you keep the written report whether or not you file.

h1: Metal vs Asphalt Shingles in Colorado: A 30 Year Cost Comparison
title: Metal vs Asphalt Cost Colorado
description: Metal vs asphalt shingles in Colorado over 30 years: installed cost per square, Front Range lifespan, hail claims, and a worked total. Get a free estimate.
keywords: standing seam metal roof cost colorado
excerpt: Asphalt costs less on the day it goes on and more over the life of the house. Here is the real 30 year math for a Front Range home, with cost tables and the hail factor most comparisons leave out.
intro:
Every roof comparison on the internet says the same thing: asphalt is cheaper up front, metal lasts longer. Both statements are true and neither one answers the question a Colorado homeowner actually has, which is what the roof will cost over the time they own the house. The answer depends on where you live. A roof in Loveland or Fort Collins gets hit with hail most years, takes more ultraviolet exposure at 5,000 feet than a roof at sea level, sees 60 degree temperature swings in a single day, and carries snow for part of the winter. All of that shortens the life of an asphalt roof and changes the math.

This comparison uses typical 2025 to 2026 Colorado installed costs, realistic Front Range lifespans, and a worked example for a common house size. Prices vary by roof pitch, complexity, access, tear off layers, and material grade, so treat every number here as a range and get a written estimate for your actual roof.

sections.h2: What you are actually comparing
sections.html:
Asphalt shingles in this comparison means architectural (laminated) shingles, which are the standard product on most Colorado homes built since the 1990s. Three tab shingles cost less and perform worse in hail and wind, and few roofers in Northern Colorado recommend them anymore. Class 4 impact rated architectural shingles are a polymer modified upgrade within the same family and are included as a separate line.

Metal roofing means standing seam steel panels, 24 or 26 gauge, with concealed clips and a PVDF (Kynar 500 type) paint finish. That is the system we install on most homes. Metal shingles and stone coated steel sit between the two in price and offer a shingle or shake look where an HOA will not approve a vertical panel. Exposed fastener panels, the corrugated product on barns and shops, cost less than standing seam but need their gasketed screws inspected over time and are not what most homeowners mean when they say metal roof.

The paint finish on metal matters for a 30 year comparison. PVDF coatings carry manufacturer chalk and fade warranties that typically run 30 to 35 years, while the less expensive silicone modified polyester (SMP) finish chalks and fades sooner, especially in dark colors under high altitude sun. A standing seam roof priced with SMP paint is not the same product as one priced with PVDF, and the two can differ by $1 to $3 per square foot. Ask which one is in your bid. Our standing seam page covers the panel and clip options in more detail.

sections.h2: Upfront installed cost in Colorado
sections.html:
Roofing is priced per square, which is 100 square feet of roof surface. A 2,000 square foot single story ranch with a moderate pitch and overhangs usually has 25 to 30 squares of roof. The ranges below reflect typical 2025 to 2026 Colorado pricing for a full tear off and replacement on a walkable roof of average complexity. Steep, cut up, or multi story roofs run higher, and Denver and Boulder metro pricing tends to sit above Northern Colorado.

SystemTypical installed cost per square25 square roof
Architectural asphalt shingles$450 to $700$11,000 to $17,500
Class 4 impact rated asphalt$550 to $850$14,000 to $21,000
Metal shingles or stone coated steel$900 to $1,400$22,500 to $35,000
Standing seam steel, PVDF finish$1,100 to $1,700$27,500 to $42,500

Those numbers include tear off and disposal of one layer, synthetic underlayment, ice and water shield at eaves and valleys as Colorado code requires, drip edge, ridge venting, and standard flashing. They do not include decking replacement, which runs extra when the inspection finds rotted or delaminated sheathing, or snow retention on metal, which most mountain and many Front Range homes should have over entries and walkways.

The upfront gap is real: standing seam typically costs two to two and a half times what architectural asphalt costs on the same roof. The rest of this article is about whether that gap closes over 30 years, and on the Front Range it usually does.

sections.h2: Lifespan in Colorado conditions
sections.html:
Manufacturers market architectural shingles as 30 year or lifetime products. On the Front Range, the realistic service life of a standard architectural shingle roof is closer to 15 to 22 years, and many are replaced sooner because of hail. There are three reasons. Ultraviolet intensity rises with altitude, and UV is what dries out the asphalt and loosens the granules. Daily temperature swings of 40 to 60 degrees cycle the shingles through expansion and contraction thousands of times. And hail, which strips granules and fractures the mat, ages a roof in a single afternoon.

Class 4 shingles stretch that life because their polymer modified asphalt stays flexible longer and absorbs impacts better. Expect 20 to 28 years on the Front Range, with a better chance of surviving a hail season without a claim.

A standing seam steel roof with a PVDF finish has a realistic service life of 40 to 70 years in Colorado. The steel does not dry out, the granules cannot wash off because there are none, and the concealed fasteners do not back out. The paint finish is the first thing to age, and PVDF chalk and fade warranties of 30 to 35 years tell you how long the color will hold up under the sun. Hail dents a steel panel at larger sizes, but a dent is cosmetic, and the roof keeps shedding water. Snow slides off a metal roof, which is why it is the default in the mountain towns, and the Class A fire rating satisfies wildfire interface codes.

Over a 30 year window, then, an asphalt roof will be replaced at least once and often twice, while a metal roof will be installed once and still have decades left. That single fact drives the math.

sections.h2: The 30 year math for a 25 square roof
sections.html:
The table below walks a 25 square Front Range roof through 30 years. It uses the midpoints of the installed cost ranges above, holds prices flat rather than guessing at inflation, and assumes the asphalt roof is replaced at year 15 and again at year 30 with one hail claim in between. Repairs cover the small items that come up on any roof: a pipe boot, a lifted shingle after a wind event, resealing a flashing. Deductible figures assume a 1 percent wind and hail deductible on a $500,000 dwelling limit, which is $5,000 per claim. Your deductible may be a flat dollar amount or a different percentage.

A few things stand out. The standard asphalt roof costs the most over 30 years even though it costs the least on day one, and that total goes up with every hail claim. Class 4 asphalt is the wild card: if it survives the hail seasons and goes 25 years, it is the cheapest option, and if it does not, it looks like standard asphalt with a higher starting price. Standing seam costs the most on day one, roughly the same as asphalt over 30 years, and is the only option with decades of life left at the end of the window. Material prices rise over time, which widens the gap in metal's favor, because the second and third asphalt roofs are bought at future prices.

sections.h2: The hail and insurance factor
sections.html:
Insurance changes this comparison in ways most calculators ignore. Colorado carriers have responded to a decade of hail losses by raising premiums, moving many policies to percentage wind and hail deductibles of 1 to 2 percent of the dwelling limit, and adding roof payment schedules or actual cash value roof endorsements that pay less as a roof ages. Under a typical roof schedule, a 15 year old asphalt roof might be reimbursed at 50 or 60 percent of replacement cost. Under an actual cash value endorsement, the same roof might be paid at a fraction of that. Either way, the second asphalt roof in the table above may be mostly out of pocket even with a claim.

A Class 4 roof, whether asphalt or metal, usually earns a premium discount. Carriers in Colorado commonly file credits in the 5 to 35 percent range on the dwelling or wind and hail portion of the premium, and you have to apply for it with the manufacturer's certification and the installation invoice. Our post on Class 4 insurance discounts explains the application and the catches.

The catch for metal is the cosmetic damage exclusion. Some carriers pair a Class 4 credit on metal with an endorsement that excludes dents that do not affect function. That is a reasonable trade for most owners, because a dented steel roof still works, but it means you should not expect a new roof after a hail storm. Ask your agent to show you the endorsement before you choose.

sections.h2: Other factors that tip the decision
sections.html:
• How long you will own the house. If you plan to sell within five years, asphalt usually wins on cost unless the buyer pool in your neighborhood expects metal. If you are staying twenty years or more, metal almost always wins.
  • HOA and architectural review. Many Front Range HOAs restrict vertical panels but accept metal shingles or stone coated steel. Get the guidelines in writing before pricing.
  • Snow and ice. Metal sheds snow, which protects the roof and loads the ground below. Snow guards over doors, decks, and gas meters are not optional. Asphalt holds snow, which can build ice dams at the eaves without proper ventilation and ice shield.
  • Wildfire exposure. Steel is noncombustible and satisfies Class A assembly requirements in Boulder County, Larimer County foothills, and the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code zones. Asphalt is also Class A as an assembly, so both qualify; the difference is ember behavior at the edges and vents.
  • Solar. Standing seam accepts clamp on racking with no roof penetrations, which solar installers prefer. Asphalt needs flashed penetrations and may need to be replaced before the panels wear out.
  • Noise and heat. Over solid decking and underlayment, a metal roof is no louder in rain than asphalt, and a light PVDF finish reflects more summer heat than a dark shingle.
  • Financing. The upfront gap is the real barrier for many owners. Financing spreads the cost of a metal roof over the years it is saving you a replacement.

The short version: if your house is on the Front Range and you plan to keep it, standing seam metal costs about the same as asphalt over 30 years and leaves you with a roof instead of a replacement bill. If you are selling soon or your HOA will not allow it, a Class 4 architectural shingle with the insurance discount applied is the strongest asphalt option. Either way, get both priced side by side on the same written estimate.

faq.q: How much more does a metal roof cost than shingles in Colorado?
faq.a: On the same house, standing seam steel with a PVDF finish typically runs $1,100 to $1,700 per square installed, versus $450 to $700 per square for architectural asphalt, so roughly two to two and a half times the upfront price. Metal shingles and stone coated steel land in between. Pitch, complexity, access, and decking condition move all of those numbers, so get a written estimate on your actual roof.

faq.q: How long does an asphalt shingle roof really last on the Front Range?
faq.a: Plan on 15 to 22 years for a standard architectural shingle, even when the package says 30 years or lifetime. Higher ultraviolet exposure at altitude, large daily temperature swings, and regular hail all shorten shingle life in Northern Colorado. Class 4 impact rated shingles usually go longer, often 20 to 28 years, because the polymer modified asphalt stays flexible and absorbs hail better.

faq.q: Does a metal roof lower homeowners insurance in Colorado?
faq.a: Often, if the panels carry a UL 2218 Class 4 rating and you submit the documentation. Colorado carriers commonly offer credits in the 5 to 35 percent range on the dwelling or wind and hail portion of the premium. Some pair the credit with a cosmetic damage exclusion that removes coverage for dents that do not affect function. Ask your agent for the endorsement language before you decide.

faq.q: Is a metal roof loud when it rains or hails?
faq.a: Not when it is installed over solid decking with underlayment, which is how residential standing seam is done. The old barn roof sound comes from panels screwed to open purlins with nothing underneath. On a house, the decking, underlayment, attic, and insulation absorb the sound, and most owners report rain noise similar to an asphalt roof. Large hail is audible on any roof.

faq.q: Can I put a metal roof over my existing shingles?
faq.a: Some jurisdictions allow one layer of shingles to remain under a metal roof, and the practice saves tear off cost. We generally recommend against it in Colorado. Leaving the old roof on hides decking damage, traps moisture, prevents a proper ice and water shield installation at the eaves, and can void manufacturer warranties. A full tear off also lets the inspector find and replace rotted sheathing before the new roof goes on.

h1: Class 4 Impact Resistant Shingles and Colorado Insurance Discounts
title: Class 4 Shingles CO Discounts
description: Class 4 impact resistant shingles in Colorado: the UL 2218 test, IBHS ratings, 5 to 35 percent insurance discounts, and how to claim one. Get a free quote.
keywords: class 4 impact resistant shingles colorado insurance discount
excerpt: Class 4 shingles pass a 2 inch steel ball test and earn premium credits from most Colorado carriers. Here is what the rating really means, what it does not, and how to get the discount.
intro:
If you have priced a roof replacement in Northern Colorado in the last few years, someone has told you to upgrade to Class 4 shingles for the insurance discount. The advice is generally sound. Class 4 is the highest impact rating under the UL 2218 standard, most Colorado carriers offer a premium credit for it, and the upgrade cost on a typical house is modest compared to the price of the roof. But the rating is narrower than the marketing suggests, the discounts vary widely between carriers, and some insurers have attached conditions that change what you get when the next storm hits.

This guide explains what the test actually measures, what the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety found when it tested the shingles under conditions closer to real hail, how the Colorado discounts work, and the paperwork needed to claim one. If you are comparing materials for a roof replacement, read this before you sign.

sections.h2: What the UL 2218 test actually measures
sections.html:
UL 2218 is a laboratory impact test published by Underwriters Laboratories. A steel ball is dropped from a fixed height onto a shingle sample mounted on a deck, twice in the same spot, at several locations including edges and joints. The sample is then flexed and examined from the back under light. If the mat has cracked or torn so that light passes through, or the shingle has split, it fails. There are four classes, defined by the ball size and drop height.

ClassSteel ball diameterDrop heightRough hail equivalent
Class 11.25 inch12 feetHalf dollar
Class 21.50 inch15 feetWalnut
Class 31.75 inch17 feetGolf ball
Class 42.00 inch20 feetLarger than golf ball

Two things are worth noticing. First, the test is pass or fail on cracking. It does not measure granule loss, dents, or how the shingle looks afterward. Second, a steel ball is harder and denser than ice, so the test is conservative on fracture energy but says nothing about the way real hail scours granules off a surface. A shingle can pass Class 4 and still lose a lot of its protective granules in a hail storm. The rating is also by product, not by installation, so the same shingle on a poorly ventilated roof over a worn deck will not perform the way the lab sample did.

Asphalt shingles reach Class 4 by modifying the asphalt with polymers, usually SBS rubber, so the mat flexes rather than cracks. The same rating is available on metal shingles, stone coated steel, standing seam panels, synthetic slate and shake, and some concrete tile, and the insurance discounts apply to those products too.

sections.h2: What IBHS found when it tested with ice
sections.html:
The Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety, a research lab funded by the insurance industry, built a different test. Instead of dropping steel balls, IBHS fires laboratory made hailstones at shingle samples at realistic speeds and then grades three kinds of damage: dents and ridges, tears, and granule loss. The lab publishes a scorecard every two years, rating each product Excellent, Good, Marginal, or Poor, and now assigns a numerical score as well.

The fourth edition, released in November 2025, covered a record 24 impact resistant products, which IBHS says represents about 95 percent of the impact resistant shingles sold each year. Most products earned Good, none earned Excellent, and IBHS states plainly that it does not recommend any product rated Marginal or Poor for use in areas that get hail. The lab added Class 3 products to the test that year, and some of those scored as well as Class 4 products, which has prompted debate in the roofing industry about how well either test predicts real roofs.

The practical lesson for a Colorado homeowner is simple. Class 4 is the entry ticket for the insurance discount, but not all Class 4 shingles perform the same in hail, and granule loss is where the differences show up. Before choosing a product, look up its IBHS rating. Choose one rated Good or better, and ask your roofer why they recommend that particular shingle over the others on the list. Our hail damage team has seen most of these products after real storms and can tell you how they held up.

sections.h2: How the Colorado discounts work
sections.html:
Colorado does not require insurers to offer an impact resistant roof discount, but most carriers writing homeowners policies here file one with the Division of Insurance. The typical credit is somewhere between 5 and 35 percent, and the important detail is what the percentage applies to. Some carriers discount the full dwelling premium. Others apply it only to the wind and hail portion, which is a smaller base. A 25 percent credit on wind and hail coverage can be worth less than a 10 percent credit on the whole dwelling premium.

Hail drives a large share of what Colorado homeowners pay. The state insurance commissioner has estimated that hail accounts for half or more of homeowner premiums in Colorado, and the average Colorado premium has risen sharply since 2019. That is why carriers are willing to pay for a roof that files fewer claims, and it is why the discounts tend to be larger here than in states with less hail.

To qualify, the carrier generally wants the following:

  • The manufacturer's UL 2218 Class 4 certification for the exact product installed, by product name and often by color.
  • The roofing contractor's invoice showing the product, the installation date, and the full roof replacement.
  • A completed impact resistant roof form from the carrier, sometimes signed by the contractor.
  • Photographs of the finished roof and sometimes of the shingle bundle labels.

The discount usually applies from the next renewal or from the date you submit the form, not retroactively. It also usually requires a full replacement; a repair with Class 4 shingles on one slope does not qualify.

sections.h2: The catches to read for
sections.html:
Carriers have responded to Colorado's hail losses in ways that interact with the Class 4 credit. Read your policy for these three endorsements before you decide the discount is worth it.

Cosmetic damage exclusion. This endorsement removes coverage for hail damage that changes the appearance of the roof without affecting its function. It is common on metal roofs and increasingly offered on Class 4 shingle roofs, sometimes as a condition of the discount. The logic is that a Class 4 roof is supposed to survive hail with cosmetic marks only, so the carrier does not want to pay for marks. The risk to you is that a Class 4 shingle roof that loses heavy granules in a storm may be called cosmetic damage and denied.

Roof payment schedule or actual cash value roof endorsement. These reduce what the carrier pays for a roof claim as the roof ages. A schedule might pay 100 percent of replacement cost in the first few years and 60 percent at 12 years. An actual cash value endorsement pays depreciated value only. Some carriers now apply these automatically once a roof reaches 10, 15, or 20 years, depending on the carrier. A Class 4 roof may be exempt from the schedule or may get a longer runway, so ask.

Percentage wind and hail deductibles. Many Colorado policies set the wind and hail deductible at 1, 2, or 5 percent of the dwelling coverage. On a $500,000 dwelling limit, a 2 percent deductible is $10,000 per claim, which is most of the cost of an asphalt roof. Colorado law at C.R.S. 6-22-105 prohibits a roofer from paying, waiving, or rebating that deductible, so the number in your policy is the number you will pay.

The Colorado Division of Insurance publishes consumer guidance on reading these endorsements and takes complaints when a carrier applies one unfairly. The insurance claim roofing page covers how we document a roof so the claim turns on the facts.

sections.h2: Does the upgrade pay for itself?
sections.html:
On most Northern Colorado homes the answer is yes, but the payback period depends on your premium and your carrier's credit. The table below uses a 25 square roof and typical 2025 to 2026 Colorado pricing, with the Class 4 upgrade costing roughly $100 to $150 more per square than standard architectural shingles.

ScenarioUpgrade costAnnual premiumCreditAnnual savingSimple payback
Small credit, moderate premium$2,500 to $3,750$3,0005 percent of dwelling$15017 to 25 years
Typical credit, typical premium$2,500 to $3,750$4,00015 percent of dwelling$6004 to 6 years
Large credit, high premium$2,500 to $3,750$5,00030 percent of dwelling$1,5002 to 3 years
Credit on wind and hail portion only$2,500 to $3,750$4,000 (half is wind and hail)25 percent of wind and hail$5005 to 8 years

The premium saving is only part of the value. The larger benefit is the claims you do not file. A Class 4 roof that comes through two hail seasons with cosmetic marks instead of functional damage saves you a deductible each time, keeps the roof off the carrier's claim history, and avoids the depreciation hit that a roof payment schedule would take on an older standard roof. Add those together and the upgrade is usually the best few thousand dollars in the whole roofing budget.

Where it does not pay off: a house you will sell within a couple of years, a carrier that offers a small credit on the wind and hail portion only, or a roof that is mostly flat or low slope where shingles are the wrong product anyway.

sections.h2: How to claim the discount, step by step
sections.html:
1. Call your agent before the roof goes on. Ask three questions: what credit does the carrier offer, what does the percentage apply to, and does accepting it add a cosmetic damage exclusion or any other endorsement. Get the answer in writing.
  2. Confirm the exact product qualifies. Carriers keep lists. A shingle line may be Class 4 in one product name and Class 3 in another from the same manufacturer. Give your agent the product name from the estimate.
  3. Check the IBHS rating. Pick a product rated Good or better, not just one that passes UL 2218.
  4. Replace the whole roof. Partial replacement does not qualify. Keep the written estimate and invoice showing the product, color, and installation date.
  5. Collect the documentation. The manufacturer's Class 4 certification letter or specification sheet, the invoice, the carrier's form, and photographs of the finished roof and bundle labels.
  6. Submit and confirm. Send the package to your agent, ask for confirmation that the credit has been applied, and check the next declarations page to be sure it shows.
  7. Keep the file. If you change carriers, you will need the same documentation again. Our written estimates and photo documented installations are built so you have it.

If you want the numbers for your own roof, request a free inspection and we will price standard and Class 4 options side by side on the same estimate.

faq.q: What does Class 4 impact resistant actually mean?
faq.a: It means the product passed the UL 2218 test at its highest level: a 2 inch steel ball dropped from 20 feet onto the sample, twice in the same spot, with no cracking or splitting of the mat when examined from the back under light. The test measures fracture resistance only. It does not grade granule loss or appearance, which is why the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety runs a separate ice impact test and publishes its own ratings.

faq.q: How much is the Class 4 shingle insurance discount in Colorado?
faq.a: Carriers filing in Colorado commonly offer credits between 5 and 35 percent. The key detail is the base: some apply the percentage to the whole dwelling premium, others only to the wind and hail portion. On a typical Northern Colorado premium that works out to a few hundred dollars a year, sometimes more. Ask your agent for the exact credit, the base it applies to, and any endorsements that come with it.

faq.q: Will a Class 4 roof stop all hail damage?
faq.a: No. Class 4 shingles resist fracturing far better than standard shingles and usually survive golf ball hail with cosmetic marks, but they can still lose granules in a severe storm, and hail over 2 inches can damage any roofing product. Ridge caps, vents, pipe boots, and flashing are also not rated and can be damaged while the field shingles are fine. The rating lowers your odds of a claim; it does not eliminate them.

faq.q: Does the discount apply to metal, tile, or synthetic roofs?
faq.a: Usually, if the specific product carries a UL 2218 Class 4 listing. Many standing seam steel panels, metal shingles, stone coated steel systems, synthetic slate and shake products, and some concrete tiles are listed. Submit the same documentation: manufacturer certification, invoice, and the carrier's form. Be aware that carriers often pair the credit on metal roofs with a cosmetic damage exclusion, so dents without functional damage may not be covered.

faq.q: Can my roofer get the discount for me?
faq.a: The application goes to your carrier through you or your agent, but a good roofer makes it easy. We provide the manufacturer's Class 4 certification for the product installed, an itemized invoice with the product name and installation date, and photographs of the finished roof. Some carrier forms ask for a contractor signature, which we provide. What we cannot do is pay or waive your deductible, which Colorado law prohibits.

h1: What to Do After a Hail Storm in Northern Colorado
title: After a Hail Storm Checklist CO
description: What to do after a hail storm in Northern Colorado: a 72 hour checklist, what to tell your adjuster, roofing law, and storm chaser red flags. Call us.
keywords: what to do after a hail storm northern colorado
excerpt: The hours after a hail storm decide how your claim goes. Here is a step by step timeline from the first evening through the adjuster meeting, with the Colorado laws that protect you.
intro:
Hail season in Northern Colorado runs from mid April into September, and in a typical year Loveland, Fort Collins, Greeley, and Windsor each see at least one storm with hail of an inch or more. When it happens, the door knockers arrive within hours, your neighbors start trading adjuster stories, and it is hard to know what to do first. The good news is that the right sequence is simple and most of it happens in the first three days.

This checklist is organized by time: the first evening, the first 72 hours, the inspection and claim, the adjuster visit, and what to do if the claim is denied or underpaid. It also explains the Colorado laws that protect homeowners from roofing fraud and from unreasonable insurers. If you have an active leak right now, skip to the safety steps and call our storm damage line at (970) 430-5884 for emergency tarping.

sections.h2: The first evening: safety and evidence
sections.html:
Nothing about your roof needs to be decided tonight. What you need to do is stay safe and preserve evidence that will melt or wash away.

  1. Check for active leaks. Walk every room and look at ceilings, especially around light fixtures, chimneys, and skylights. Check the attic with a flashlight if you can do so safely. Put buckets under drips and move anything valuable.
  2. Do not go on the roof. Wet shingles with granule loss are slick, and foot traffic on bruised shingles adds damage an adjuster can later attribute to you rather than the storm.
  3. Photograph hailstones. If stones are still on the ground, set a few next to a ruler or a coin and photograph them. Put several in a freezer bag. Melted hail cannot be measured, and size is the first thing an adjuster asks about.
  4. Photograph soft metals and property. Gutters, downspouts, window screens, air conditioner fins, the grill, the mailbox, the deck, the cars. Everything that is dented is proof of the storm's intensity at your address.
  5. Write down the details. Date, time, duration, wind direction, and the size the hail appeared to be. Screenshot any weather alerts on your phone.
  6. If water is coming in, call for a tarp. Emergency tarping is a covered mitigation expense under most policies. Keep the receipt.

Do not sign anything tonight. Anyone who knocks on your door the evening of a storm with a contract in hand is working their own timeline, not yours.

sections.h2: The first 72 hours: inspection and policy review
sections.html:
The next three days are about finding out whether you have a claim and understanding what your policy will do with it. Do these in order.

Read your policy. Find the declarations page and the conditions section. You are looking for four things: your wind and hail deductible, whether it is a flat dollar amount or a percentage of the dwelling limit; whether the roof is covered at replacement cost or actual cash value, or under a roof payment schedule; whether there is a cosmetic damage exclusion; and the notice deadline, which often requires prompt notice and sometimes sets a one year window for wind and hail claims. Our post on whether insurance covers roof replacement explains each of these.

Get a professional inspection. Schedule a free, photo documented inspection with a local, licensed roofer. The inspector walks every slope, marks test squares, counts hits, photographs damage to the field shingles and to every accessory, and gives you a written report. You keep the report whether or not you file. If the inspector tells you the roof does not have claimable damage, that is useful information too. Our free inspection is built for exactly this.

Decide whether to file. Compare the inspector's findings to your deductible. If the damage is a few hits on one slope and your deductible is $5,000, a claim may not make sense and could affect your rates. If the roof has functional damage across multiple slopes, file. The decision is yours; a roofer should not file for you or pressure you to file.

File promptly. Call your carrier or use its app. You will get a claim number and an adjuster assignment, usually within a few days to two weeks after a major storm. Write the claim number on the inspection report.

sections.h2: What to say to your adjuster, and what not to say
sections.html:
The adjuster works for the carrier and is trained to find the facts and apply the policy. Your job is to give accurate information and to make sure the adjuster sees everything. Here is what helps and what hurts.

Say this:

  • The date and approximate time of the storm, and the hail size you observed or photographed.
  • That you have a written inspection report with photographs and you would like the adjuster to review it.
  • That you would like your roofer present at the inspection to point out the damage found. Most adjusters welcome this. Once you have a signed contract with us, we meet the adjuster on site.
  • Specific items: the slopes, the gutters, the vents, the skylights, the screens, the fence, the air conditioner. Ask that each be inspected and listed in the scope.
  • That there was no leak or damage before the storm, if that is true.

Do not say this:

  • Guesses about cause. Do not say the roof was already old or that you think some of the damage may be from a previous storm. State what you know and let the inspection establish the rest.
  • That you are not sure whether the hail was big enough. Report what you observed and photographed.
  • That the roofer told you it would be covered. Coverage is the adjuster's determination under the policy; a roofer stating it will be covered is not evidence.
  • Anything about the deductible being handled. Colorado law prohibits a roofer from paying, waiving, or rebating your deductible, and mentioning any such arrangement can put the whole claim at risk.

Be polite and precise. Ask the adjuster for a copy of the scope and the estimate, and ask how to submit a supplement if the roofer finds additional damage during the work, which is common once the old roof is off.

sections.h2: Storm chasers and the Colorado roofing law that protects you
sections.html:
After every significant Front Range storm, out of area roofing crews flood the neighborhoods. Some are legitimate. Many are not. Colorado's residential roofing law, Senate Bill 12-038, codified at C.R.S. 6-22-101 and following, was written because of them. Here is what it does for you.

  • Written contract required. The contract must state the scope of work, the materials, the cost, the contractor's physical address and phone number, and the approximate dates of service.
  • No deductible games. C.R.S. 6-22-105 makes it illegal for a roofing contractor to pay, waive, rebate, or promise to rebate any part of your insurance deductible. A roofer who offers to make your roof free is breaking the law and exposing you to a fraud problem with your carrier. Walk away.
  • 72 hour cancellation right. Under C.R.S. 6-22-104, if your insurer denies the claim in whole or in part, you may rescind the roofing contract within 72 hours after you receive the written denial, by written notice to the contractor's address in the contract. The contractor must return any deposit within ten days, less the value of work actually performed.
  • Deposits. A contractor may not hold your payment from the insurer until materials are delivered to the property or a substantial portion of the work is done.
  • Disclosure of insurance. The contractor must carry and disclose liability coverage.

The warning signs of a storm chaser are consistent: no local address or out of state plates and phone numbers; pressure to sign the day of the storm; a contract that assigns your insurance benefits before anyone has inspected; an offer to cover your deductible; a request for a large cash deposit before materials are ordered; no proof of insurance. A local roofer with a physical address in Larimer or Weld County will be here when the warranty matters. Our Loveland office is at 1180 E 3rd St.

sections.h2: A realistic claim timeline
sections.html:
Every claim is different, but a straightforward hail claim in Northern Colorado tends to follow this pattern. Large storms slow everything down because adjusters are handling hundreds of files.

TimingWhat happensWhat you do
Day 0StormSafety, photographs, hailstone samples, emergency tarp if leaking
Days 1 to 3Inspection and policy reviewFree roofer inspection, read deductible and roof coverage terms, decide to file
Days 3 to 14Claim filed, adjuster assignedRecord claim number, schedule adjuster visit, ask roofer to attend
Days 7 to 30Adjuster inspectionAttend, provide inspection report, request scope and estimate
Days 14 to 45Scope and first paymentCompare carrier scope to roofer estimate, flag missing code items, sign contract
Days 30 to 90Materials ordered, roof replacedMost homes are torn off and re roofed in one to two days once materials arrive
After completionFinal invoice, depreciation releasedSubmit invoice and photos to recover withheld depreciation if the policy pays replacement cost

The carrier's first check is usually the actual cash value of the roof less the deductible. The withheld depreciation is paid after you prove the work was completed at the agreed cost. If the roofer's estimate is higher than the carrier's scope because of code required items such as ice and water shield, drip edge, or ventilation, those get submitted as a supplement with photographs and code citations.

sections.h2: If the claim is denied or underpaid
sections.html:
Denials and low scopes happen, especially after big storms when adjusters are moving fast. You have options, in roughly this order.

  1. Ask for the reason in writing. The denial letter should state the policy provision relied on. Common reasons are damage attributed to wear, blistering, or a prior storm; damage called cosmetic; or hit counts below the carrier's threshold.
  2. Request a re inspection. Ask for a different adjuster, and have your roofer present with the photo report and test square counts. Many denials reverse at this stage.
  3. Invoke the appraisal clause. Most policies allow either party to demand appraisal when the dispute is about the amount of loss. Each side hires an appraiser and the two select an umpire. This resolves scope and price disputes without a lawsuit.
  4. File a complaint with the Colorado Division of Insurance. The Division reviews claim handling and can require the carrier to respond.
  5. Know the bad faith statutes. C.R.S. 10-3-1115 prohibits an insurer from unreasonably delaying or denying payment of a covered benefit. Under C.R.S. 10-3-1116, a policyholder who proves unreasonable delay or denial can recover two times the covered benefit plus attorney fees and costs. If you reach this point, talk to an attorney who handles first party insurance claims. We provide inspection reports and documentation to attorneys and public adjusters through our casualty services, but we do not negotiate claims or act as a public adjuster.

Remember the 72 hour rescission right. If the carrier denies the claim and you signed a roofing contract contingent on it, you can cancel in writing within 72 hours of receiving the denial and get your deposit back.

faq.q: Should I file a hail claim right away or wait for an inspection?
faq.a: Get the inspection first if you can do it within a few days. A written, photo documented report tells you whether the damage is worth a claim given your deductible, and it gives the adjuster something concrete to review. If the inspection finds functional damage, file promptly. Policies require prompt notice and many set a one year window for wind and hail, so do not let the decision drift past a season.

faq.q: Can a roofer pay or waive my deductible after a hail storm in Colorado?
faq.a: No. C.R.S. 6-22-105 makes it illegal for a roofing contractor to pay, waive, rebate, or promise to rebate any part of an insurance deductible. A roofer who offers it is committing a crime and inviting the carrier to treat your claim as fraud. We never do it, and you should treat the offer as the clearest sign of a storm chaser.

faq.q: What if my insurance denies the claim after I signed a roofing contract?
faq.a: Colorado's roofing law gives you a 72 hour window to cancel. Under C.R.S. 6-22-104, when the insurer denies the claim in whole or in part, you may rescind the contract by written notice to the contractor within 72 hours of receiving the written denial. The contractor must return your deposit within ten days, keeping only the value of work actually performed. Send the notice by email and keep a copy.

faq.q: Should my roofer meet the insurance adjuster?
faq.a: Yes, once you have signed a contract with that roofer. The roofer points out the hits found during the inspection, confirms the test square counts, and makes sure accessories like vents, flashing, and skylights are included in the scope. The adjuster still makes the coverage decision. A roofer should not negotiate your claim or represent you with the carrier; that is a public adjuster's role and requires a license in Colorado.

faq.q: How long after a hail storm can damage still be found?
faq.a: Hail bruises do not heal, so a competent inspector can usually identify them a year or more later. But fresh hits are easier to see and easier to prove, because the exposed asphalt is still black and shiny. Weathering turns it gray, and later storms add confusion about dates. Inspect within days of the storm, and file inside your policy's notice window, which is often one year for wind and hail.

h1: Does Homeowners Insurance Cover Roof Replacement in Colorado?
title: Does Insurance Cover a New Roof
description: Does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement in Colorado? RCV vs ACV, roof schedules, hail deductibles, and deadlines explained. Get a free inspection.
keywords: does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement colorado
excerpt: Colorado policies cover sudden damage, not worn out roofs, and the fine print decides how much you get. Here is how RCV, ACV, roof schedules, percentage deductibles, and code coverage work.
intro:
Homeowners insurance in Colorado covers roof replacement when a covered peril damages the roof, and hail and wind are the perils that matter most on the Front Range. It does not cover a roof that has simply worn out, and over the last several years carriers have added endorsements that change how much they pay even when the damage is clearly covered. Whether your claim pays for a full replacement, a depreciated fraction of one, or nothing at all depends on four things: the cause of the damage, the age of the roof, the type of roof coverage on your policy, and your deductible.

This guide explains each of those, with worked numbers, the Colorado statutes that apply, and the deadlines that quietly end claims. If you suspect storm damage, the first step is a free, photo documented inspection so you know what you are dealing with before you call the carrier.

sections.h2: What is covered and what is not
sections.html:
A standard Colorado homeowners policy (the HO-3 form is the most common) covers the dwelling against sudden and accidental direct physical loss unless a peril is excluded. For roofs, the covered perils that come up are hail, windstorm, weight of ice and snow, falling objects such as tree limbs, fire, and vandalism. If one of those damages the roof, the policy owes for the repair or replacement, subject to the deductible and the roof coverage terms discussed below.

What is not covered is just as important:

  • Wear, tear, and deterioration. A 22 year old shingle roof that is curling, cracking, and bald is not a covered loss. It is maintenance.
  • Faulty installation or defective materials. Blistering shingles, nail pops, and improperly flashed valleys are workmanship or product issues, which fall to the contractor's workmanship warranty or the manufacturer, not the carrier.
  • Neglect. A small leak that was ignored for two years until the decking rotted is generally excluded.
  • Cosmetic damage, if the policy carries a cosmetic damage exclusion endorsement. This is common on metal roofs and increasingly on impact rated shingle roofs.
  • Earth movement and flood, which are separate policies.

Carriers also scrutinize cause. If hail hits a roof that was already at the end of its life, the adjuster may argue the roof was already failed and offer little. That is where a professional inspection with test squares, hit counts, and photographs of fresh impacts matters, because it separates storm damage from age.

sections.h2: Replacement cost vs actual cash value
sections.html:
This is the single biggest variable in what a roof claim pays. Replacement cost value (RCV) coverage pays what it costs to replace the roof with like kind and quality today. Actual cash value (ACV) coverage pays replacement cost minus depreciation for age and condition. The difference on an older roof is enormous.

Example: 20 year rated asphalt roof, $20,000 to replaceRCV policyACV policy
Roof age at the storm15 years15 years
Depreciation (15 of 20 years used)$15,000, withheld but recoverable$15,000, not recoverable
First payment before deductible$5,000$5,000
Paid after the roof is replacedAdditional $15,000$0
Total before deductible$20,000$5,000

On an RCV policy the carrier usually pays in two steps. The first check is the actual cash value less your deductible. After you replace the roof and submit the invoice, the carrier releases the withheld depreciation, called recoverable depreciation. Two things trip people up here. First, most policies set a deadline, often 180 days to a year, to complete the work and claim the depreciation. Second, if you choose a cheaper roof than the one scoped, the carrier pays the lesser amount; if you choose a more expensive one, you pay the difference.

Many Colorado carriers have moved roofs to ACV through an endorsement, sometimes automatically once the roof passes 10, 15, or 20 years depending on the carrier, and sometimes at renewal for all shingle roofs. The endorsement is on your declarations page under a name like roof surfacing payment schedule or actual cash value loss settlement for roofs. If you do not know which you have, find out before hail season.

sections.h2: Roof payment schedules and roof age
sections.html:
A roof payment schedule is a middle ground that pays a fixed percentage of replacement cost based on the roof's age and material, regardless of its actual condition. A typical schedule for asphalt shingles might look like this, though every carrier's table is different and you should read your own.

Roof ageTypical percentage of replacement cost paid
0 to 5 years100 percent
6 to 10 years80 to 90 percent
11 to 15 years60 to 70 percent
16 to 20 years40 to 50 percent
Over 20 years20 to 30 percent, or ACV only

Metal, tile, and slate roofs usually get longer schedules, and some carriers exempt Class 4 impact rated roofs from the schedule entirely or extend the full payment period. That is one of the quieter reasons the Class 4 upgrade pays off in Colorado.

Roof age also affects whether you can get or keep coverage. Carriers increasingly ask for the roof's installation date at application and renewal, require an inspection on roofs over 15 or 20 years, and non renew homes with aging shingle roofs. If you receive a non renewal notice citing the roof, act on it early: a documented inspection showing remaining life, or a replacement, usually resolves it, and it is harder to find a new carrier after a lapse.

sections.h2: Deductibles, and why no roofer can waive yours
sections.html:
Colorado policies increasingly carry a separate wind and hail deductible, set as a percentage of the dwelling coverage rather than a flat amount. One, two, and five percent are common. On a $500,000 dwelling limit, that is $5,000, $10,000, or $25,000 per claim, which on a $20,000 roof means the carrier pays $15,000, $10,000, or nothing. Some carriers sell a flat dollar wind and hail buyback for extra premium. Check your declarations page for the exact figure before you assume a hail claim is worth filing.

Colorado law closes the door on the oldest trick in storm roofing. Under C.R.S. 6-22-105, a roofing contractor may not pay, waive, rebate, or promise to rebate any part of a homeowner's insurance deductible, and may not advertise that it will. The reason is simple: a roofer who absorbs the deductible is either inflating the invoice to the carrier, which is insurance fraud, or cutting the quality of the roof. We never do it, and a roofer who offers should be shown the door. The insurance claim roofing page explains how we work inside the law.

One related point: your deductible applies per claim, not per item. Hail that damages the roof, the gutters, the screens, the fence, and the air conditioner is one claim with one deductible. List everything.

sections.h2: Code upgrades, matching, and partial replacement
sections.html:
Three scope issues come up on nearly every Northern Colorado roof claim.

Code upgrade coverage. Current Colorado building codes require ice and water shield at eaves and valleys, metal drip edge, specified underlayment, and in many jurisdictions proper attic ventilation. A roof installed 20 years ago may have none of that. The carrier's base scope pays to put back what was there; ordinance or law coverage, which is included in many policies at 10 percent of the dwelling limit and available at higher limits, pays for the code required items. Make sure your policy has it and that the roofer's estimate itemizes the code items separately with the code citation, so they can be supplemented.

Matching. If hail damages the north slope only, the carrier may scope that slope alone. Colorado does not have a matching statute, so whether the undamaged slopes are replaced to match depends on the policy language and negotiation. If the shingle is discontinued and no reasonable match exists, many carriers will replace the whole roof. Documentation of the product and the lack of a match is what carries that argument.

Partial replacement. On tile, slate, and metal roofs, repair of damaged units is often possible and often what the carrier scopes. The question is whether the repair restores the roof to pre loss condition. Mismatched tiles or panels from a different production run, and damage to the underlayment underneath, are the usual reasons a repair is not adequate.

In every case the roofer's job is to document the damage and the code requirements so the scope matches the real work. Our inspections are built to do that, and the written estimate itemizes every line so you and the adjuster can compare them.

sections.h2: Deadlines, delays, and your rights under Colorado law
sections.html:
Claims die on deadlines more often than on denials. Know these.

  • Notice of loss. Policies require prompt notice. Many Colorado policies also set a contractual window, often one year from the date of loss, for wind and hail claims. Hail damage found after that window is usually not covered.
  • Recoverable depreciation. Typically 180 days to one year after the first payment to complete the work and submit the invoice.
  • Suit limitation. Policies set a period, often one to two years from the date of loss, to bring a lawsuit over the claim.
  • The 72 hour rescission right. Under C.R.S. 6-22-104, if the carrier denies the claim after you have signed a roofing contract, you may cancel the contract in writing within 72 hours of receiving the denial.

If the carrier drags its feet or denies a claim without a reasonable basis, Colorado gives you more than a breach of contract claim. C.R.S. 10-3-1115 prohibits an insurer from unreasonably delaying or denying payment of a covered benefit to a first party claimant, judged by what a reasonable insurer would have done. Under C.R.S. 10-3-1116, a policyholder who proves unreasonable delay or denial can recover two times the covered benefit plus reasonable attorney fees and costs. Before it reaches that point, request a re inspection, invoke the appraisal clause for disputes about the amount, and file a complaint with the Colorado Division of Insurance. If you hire an attorney or a licensed public adjuster, we supply inspection reports and photo documentation through our casualty services, but we do not negotiate claims and we are not public adjusters.

faq.q: Will insurance pay to replace my roof if it is just old?
faq.a: No. Homeowners insurance covers sudden damage from a covered peril such as hail, wind, or a fallen tree. Wear, deterioration, curling, and granule loss from age are maintenance and are excluded. If a storm damages an old roof, the carrier owes for the storm damage, but it may pay on an actual cash value basis or under a roof payment schedule that reflects the roof's age, which can leave most of the cost with you.

faq.q: What is recoverable depreciation on a roof claim?
faq.a: On a replacement cost policy, the carrier first pays the roof's actual cash value, which is replacement cost minus depreciation for age. The depreciation is withheld, not denied. Once you replace the roof and submit the final invoice, the carrier releases it. Most policies set a deadline, often 180 days to a year from the first payment, to finish the work and claim the depreciation, so do not let the project sit.

faq.q: How does a percentage hail deductible work in Colorado?
faq.a: The deductible is a percentage of the dwelling coverage limit, not of the claim. A 2 percent wind and hail deductible on a $500,000 dwelling limit is $10,000, deducted from whatever the carrier pays on that claim. One deductible applies per claim, so the roof, gutters, screens, and fence damaged in one storm count as a single claim. Colorado law prohibits any roofer from paying or waiving the deductible for you.

faq.q: Does insurance pay for code required items like ice and water shield?
faq.a: Only if your policy includes ordinance or law coverage, which many policies carry at 10 percent of the dwelling limit and some at higher limits. The base scope restores what was there; code coverage pays for ice and water shield, drip edge, underlayment, and ventilation that current Colorado code requires on a replacement. Ask your roofer to itemize code items separately on the estimate with the code reference so they can be supplemented.

faq.q: What can I do if the insurance company delays or lowballs my roof claim?
faq.a: Start with a written request for the reason and a re inspection with your roofer present. If the dispute is about price or scope, invoke the policy's appraisal clause. File a complaint with the Colorado Division of Insurance. If the carrier is acting without a reasonable basis, C.R.S. 10-3-1115 and 10-3-1116 allow a policyholder to recover two times the covered benefit plus attorney fees; talk to a first party insurance attorney at that stage.

h1: Best Roofing Materials for Wildfire Zones in Colorado
title: Wildfire Zone Roofing Colorado
description: Best roofing materials for wildfire zones in Colorado: Class A assemblies, the 2025 state wildfire code, ember resistant vents, cedar risks. Get a quote.
keywords: best roofing materials for wildfire zones colorado
class a fire rated roof colorado
excerpt: Embers, not flames, destroy most homes in a Colorado wildfire, and the roof is where they land. Here is how Class A ratings work, what the new state code requires, and which materials to choose.
intro:
The three fires that reshaped Colorado's thinking about homes were not forest fires that marched up to the walls. The Cameron Peak Fire in 2020 burned more than 200,000 acres of Larimer County, the largest wildfire in state history, and the East Troublesome Fire that same October ran across Grand County and into the Grand Lake area in a single night. The Marshall Fire on December 30, 2021, burned grassland in Boulder County driven by winds reported over 100 mph and destroyed 991 homes in Louisville, Superior, and unincorporated areas, most of them suburban houses miles from any forest.

What those fires had in common was embers. Burning fragments carried on the wind land on roofs, collect in gutters and valleys, blow into attic vents, and lodge under the edges of roofing. The roof is the largest surface on the house and the one most exposed to a shower of embers, which is why fire codes start there. This guide explains what a Class A rating means, what Colorado's 2025 statewide wildfire code and the county rules in Boulder and Larimer require, where embers get in, and how the common roofing materials compare. If you are in a mapped zone, our Estes Park and Nederland crews do this work every season.

sections.h2: What a Class A fire rating means
sections.html:
Roof fire ratings come from ASTM E108 and UL 790, which are the same test under two names. A roof assembly, meaning the covering plus the underlayment and deck it is installed on, is exposed to three things: a gas flame at the surface, a burning wood brand placed on it, and flame spread along the slope. Class A is the highest rating. It requires the assembly to withstand a large burning brand (about 12 inches square) without the fire penetrating to the deck, with limited flame spread and no flying brands produced by the roof itself. Class B uses a smaller brand and Class C a smaller one still.

The word assembly matters. Some materials are Class A on their own: concrete and clay tile, slate, and most metal panels are noncombustible and are listed as standalone Class A coverings. Others, including asphalt shingles and most synthetic slate and shake products, achieve Class A only as part of a tested assembly over a specified underlayment, sometimes a fire resistant cap sheet or a gypsum board layer, on a solid deck. Install the same shingle over the wrong underlayment and the roof is not Class A. Fire treated cedar shake can be Class B or, with a special underlayment, a Class A assembly, but the treatment leaches out over years of sun and rain, and untreated cedar is unrated.

Most Colorado jurisdictions in the wildland urban interface require Class A, and the building inspector will ask for the listing that shows the exact combination of covering, underlayment, and deck. A good roofer provides it with the permit application.

sections.h2: Colorado's wildfire code: what changed in 2025 and 2026
sections.html:
Until recently, wildfire construction rules in Colorado were a patchwork of county and town codes. That changed when the legislature created the Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code Board, which adopted the state's first statewide Wildfire Resiliency Code in 2025 along with a statewide map that classifies land as Low, Moderate, or High wildfire intensity. The map measures how severely a fire could burn based on vegetation, slope, and weather, not how likely one is to start, and it reaches well onto the plains. Front Range suburbs including parts of Centennial, Superior, and Louisville are mapped in Low and Moderate zones.

The code sets a minimum standard that local governments in mapped areas must adopt and enforce, with local amendments allowed. Jurisdictions have been adopting through 2026, and several set effective dates around the middle of the year. For roofs, the requirements are consistent across the zones:

  • Class A roof assembly on new construction and expansions over 500 square feet, and on existing roofs when 25 percent or more of the roof area is replaced.
  • Noncombustible gutters and downspouts, with a means of keeping leaves and needles out.
  • Ember resistant attic, eave, and foundation vents, either listed to ASTM E2886 or screened with corrosion resistant metal mesh with openings of 1/8 inch or less.
  • In Moderate and High zones, additional requirements for eaves, soffits, exterior walls, decks, and garage door sealing.

Several counties were already there. Boulder County's ignition resistant construction rules (publication B-37, code section R390) have required Class A assemblies in both of its wildfire zones for years, along with metal drip edge so no sheathing is exposed, noncombustible gutters, 1/8 inch vent mesh, corrosion resistant metal valleys over 36 inch underlayment, fire stopping of the open space at the eaves under profiled roofing, and tempered or rated skylight glazing. Summit County and the Town of Breckenridge prohibit wood shake roofs. Larimer County applies wildfire hazard review in the foothills and around Estes Park, Red Feather Lakes, Glen Haven, and Drake. The practical rule: if your address is in the mountains, the foothills, or a mapped grassland interface, plan on Class A and ember resistant details whether or not the inspector asks.

sections.h2: Where embers get in
sections.html:
Research from the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety and post fire investigations in Colorado point to the same entry points over and over. A Class A roof covering does nothing if an ember gets past it.

  • Attic and gable vents. Standard louvered vents with 1/4 inch screen let embers straight into the attic, where they land on dry framing and insulation. Replace with ember resistant vents listed to ASTM E2886 or screen with 1/8 inch metal mesh. This is the single highest value upgrade on an existing house.
  • Gutters. Pine needles and leaves in a gutter are kindling placed against the fascia. Vinyl gutters melt and drop burning debris against the wall. Use metal gutters with metal guards and keep them clean.
  • Roof edges and eaves. Exposed sheathing at the drip edge and open soffits catch embers. Metal drip edge over the sheathing and enclosed, noncombustible soffits close them.
  • The gap under profiled roofing. Barrel tile, high rib metal, and shake leave openings at the eave and ridge. Embers blow into the space and ignite the underlayment or the deck. Bird stops, foam closures, or a cap sheet layer seal those openings and are required in Boulder County.
  • Valleys and roof to wall intersections. Debris collects there. Metal valleys and metal flashing at every wall keep an ember from finding wood.
  • Skylights. Plastic domes melt and open a hole. Use tempered or multi layer glass.
  • Roof mounted equipment. Swamp coolers and satellite mounts create pockets that trap debris.

When we re roof a home in a wildfire zone, the vent, gutter, edge, and closure details are part of the scope, because that is where the house is actually lost.

sections.h2: How the roofing materials compare
sections.html:
Every material below can be part of a Class A roof. They differ in how they get there, how they handle embers at the edges, and how they perform against Colorado's other hazards, because a wildfire zone roof in Estes Park also carries snow and takes hail.

Concrete or clay tileClass A, noncombustibleGood only with bird stops and sealed hips and ridges; open barrel ends are a known ember trapHeavy, cracks in large hail; structural check needed$1,000 to $1,500
