Costs are typical Colorado ranges for 2025 to 2026 and vary with pitch, complexity, access, and decking condition; mountain projects usually run higher than the Front Range because of access and weather days. For most wildfire zone homes the choice comes down to standing seam metal, which is the mountain default for fire, snow, and hail together, and synthetic shake or slate, which gives the traditional look that HOAs and historic districts in places like Estes Park often want without the fuel load. Our synthetic roofing page covers those products and their Class A listings.

sections.h2: The cedar shake problem
sections.html:
Cedar shake is the roof most of Colorado's mountain homes were built with, and it is the roof the fires keep finding. Weathered cedar is dry, split, and full of gaps that catch embers, and a shake roof that catches produces its own flying brands that light the neighbors. Fire retardant treatments help when new, but the chemicals leach out with sun and rain over the years, and there is no practical way to retreat a roof in place. Insurance carriers know this: many will not write or renew a policy on a cedar shake roof in a mapped wildfire zone, and those that do charge for it.

If you have cedar now, you have three paths. Replace it with a Class A system, which is what the 2025 state code will require whenever 25 percent or more of the roof is redone, and what Summit County, Breckenridge, and other jurisdictions already require outright. Replace it with synthetic shake, which looks like cedar from the street, carries Class A and Class 4 listings, and weighs about the same. Or keep it and harden everything around it: 1/8 inch mesh on every vent, metal gutters and guards, metal drip edge, defensible space, and a plan to replace it at the next hail claim. Honest advice: the third option is a bridge, not a destination. Our cedar shake page explains when cedar still makes sense outside the interface and what the Class A assembly options are.

sections.h2: Choosing for your property
sections.html:
Work through these in order and the choice usually makes itself.

  1. Find your zone. Check the state wildfire intensity map and your county's wildfire zone map. Boulder County, Larimer County, Summit County, Grand County, and the Estes Park and Nederland areas all have mapped zones with their own requirements. Ask the permit office what it will inspect for.
  2. Check your insurance. Ask your agent whether the carrier has conditions on roofing material in your zone, and whether a Class A noncombustible roof earns a credit. Some do.
  3. Decide on look and weight. Standing seam and metal shingles are light and can go on almost any structure. Tile and slate need an engineer's check of the framing. Synthetic shake and slate give the traditional look at shingle weight.
  4. Price the whole assembly. Get the Class A listing for the exact covering and underlayment combination, and make sure ember resistant vents, metal gutters, drip edge, closures, and skylight glazing are itemized on the estimate. A low bid that leaves those out is not the same roof.
  5. Think about hail and snow at the same time. A Class 4 rating and proper snow retention cost little extra at install and save a lot later. Our mountain roofing guide covers the snow side.
  6. Handle the yard too. The best roof in the county will not survive a propane tank, a wood pile, or a juniper hedge against the wall. Five feet of noncombustible ground around the house is the companion to the roof.

We inspect wildfire zone roofs for free, with photographs of every vent, edge, and gap, and a written report of what current code and your insurer are likely to require. That report is useful whether you re roof this year or in five.

faq.q: What is the best roof for a wildfire zone in Colorado?
faq.a: Standing seam steel is the most common answer for mountain and foothills homes because it is noncombustible, Class A on its own, sheds snow, and is available with Class 4 hail ratings. Metal shingles, stone coated steel, synthetic slate and shake, concrete tile, and natural slate all reach Class A as well. The right choice depends on the structure's weight capacity, HOA or historic district rules, snow exposure, and budget.

faq.q: Are asphalt shingles allowed in Colorado wildfire zones?
faq.a: Yes. Asphalt shingles installed over a standard underlayment on a solid deck are a Class A assembly and satisfy the roof covering requirement in most Colorado jurisdictions, including the 2025 state wildfire code. Choose a Class 4 impact rated product for hail, and pay attention to the ember details that shingles do not address on their own: metal drip edge, ember resistant vents, metal gutters, and sealed eaves and soffits.

faq.q: Does the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code apply to my existing roof?
faq.a: Not until you work on it. The code applies to new construction, additions over 500 square feet, and existing roofs when 25 percent or more of the roof area is replaced, at which point a Class A assembly, noncombustible gutters, and ember resistant vents are required. Local governments in mapped zones are adopting the code through 2026 and may add local amendments, so confirm the effective date and requirements with your permit office before you re roof.

faq.q: Can I keep my cedar shake roof in a Colorado wildfire zone?
faq.a: In some jurisdictions, until you replace it; in others, such as Summit County and Breckenridge, wood shake is prohibited. Even where it is allowed, fire retardant treatment wears off, insurers increasingly decline cedar roofs in mapped zones, and the state code requires a Class A assembly when a quarter or more of the roof is redone. Hardening the vents, gutters, and edges buys time. Synthetic shake gives the same look with Class A and Class 4 listings.

faq.q: What are ember resistant vents and do I need them?
faq.a: They are attic, gable, eave, and foundation vents designed to block burning embers and flame, either listed to the ASTM E2886 test or built with corrosion resistant metal mesh with openings of 1/8 inch or less. Standard louvered vents with 1/4 inch screen let embers straight into the attic, which is one of the most common ways homes ignite. Boulder County and the 2025 state code require them, and they are the highest value upgrade on an existing house.

h1: How Long Does a Roof Last in Colorado?
title: How Long a Roof Lasts in Colorado
description: How long a roof lasts in Colorado by material, from 3-tab shingles to slate, and what hail, UV, and freeze-thaw do to those numbers. Get a free inspection.
keywords: how long does a roof last in colorado
excerpt: Manufacturer lifespans assume a mild climate. Colorado is not one. Here is how long each roofing material really lasts on the Front Range and in the mountains, and how to tell where yours is.
intro:
Ask a shingle manufacturer how long its product lasts and you will hear a warranty number. Ask a roofer who has torn off a few hundred roofs between Loveland and Fort Collins and you will hear a shorter one. Both are honest. The difference is the climate. Colorado roofs live with high-altitude ultraviolet exposure, hail that arrives most years between April and September, freeze-thaw cycling that can cross 32 degrees several times in one spring day, and wind events that break shingle seals along the foothills. Every one of those takes years off the number on the wrapper.

This guide gives realistic service-life ranges for the materials we see on Colorado homes, explains what shortens or extends them, and lays out a simple way to decide whether your roof has a decade left or is already a liability with your insurance carrier.

sections.h2: Why Colorado shortens roof life
sections.html:
Four forces age a Colorado roof faster than the same roof in Ohio or Oregon.

  • Ultraviolet at altitude. Loveland sits near 5,000 feet, Estes Park near 7,500, and the resort towns above 8,000. Thinner air filters less UV, and the state sees roughly 300 days of sun a year. UV cooks the oils out of asphalt, which is why shingles here curl, lose granules, and go brittle earlier than their rating suggests.
  • Hail. The Front Range is the core of what the insurance industry calls Hail Alley. State insurance regulators reported more than 800 storms with hail of one inch or larger in 2023 alone. A roof does not have to be destroyed by hail to be aged by it. Repeated small hail bruises the mat and knocks granules loose, and the damage compounds.
  • Freeze-thaw cycling. A sunny February afternoon at 50 degrees followed by a night at 15 degrees moves water in and out of every crack in a roof. Tile, slate, and concrete products that absorb water suffer most. Asphalt sealant strips fatigue and release.
  • Wind. Downslope winds along the foothills regularly exceed 60 miles per hour. Once a shingle's seal strip breaks, each gust works the tab a little looser until it tears or lets water under the course above it.

Snow load matters too, mainly in the mountains, where it stresses structure and drives ice dams. We cover that in our guide to mountain roofing above 8,000 feet.

sections.h2: Roof lifespan by material in Colorado
sections.html:
The ranges below reflect what we see on Colorado roofs, not laboratory ratings. The low end assumes a basic installation and a hail-prone location such as Greeley or Windsor. The high end assumes correct installation, ventilation, and maintenance.

MaterialRealistic Colorado service lifeWhat usually ends it
3-tab asphalt shingle15 to 20 yearsHail, granule loss, wind lift
Architectural (laminated) shingle20 to 30 yearsHail, UV embrittlement
Class 4 impact-resistant shingle20 to 30 yearsUV and age; hail far less often
Standing seam metal (PVDF finish)40 to 70 yearsFastener and sealant fatigue, finish chalking
Stone-coated steel40 to 60 yearsUnderlayment failure, coating wear
Concrete tile50 years or moreUnderlayment failure, freeze-thaw spalling, breakage
Clay tile75 years or moreUnderlayment and flashing, hail breakage
Natural slate (hard S1 grade)75 to 150 years or moreNails and flashings, not the stone
Cedar shake20 to 35 years with maintenanceUV splitting, moss, fire code restrictions
Synthetic slate or shake (polymer)40 to 50 yearsAge; most carry Class 4 and Class A ratings
TPO single-ply (low slope)20 to 30 yearsSeam failure, UV, hail punctures
EPDM rubber (low slope)20 to 30 yearsSeam and flashing failure, shrinkage
Fluid-applied roof coating10 to 20 years, then recoatFilm erosion; recoat extends it

Two patterns in that table deserve a closer look. First, the three cheapest systems are also the three most likely to be replaced after a hail claim, which is why Class 4 shingles earn insurance discounts in Colorado. Second, every long-lived material fails at its weakest component, not its surface. Tile, slate, and stone-coated steel all ride on an underlayment that lasts 30 to 50 years, so the roof you think is a 75-year roof may need a lift-and-relay at year 40.

sections.h2: What shortens or extends those numbers
sections.html:
Two identical houses on the same street in Loveland can have roofs that die 10 years apart. The difference is almost always one of these.

Installation quality

Nail placement, nail count, starter strip, and sealed valleys determine whether an architectural shingle survives its first 90 mile per hour gust. High-nailed or under-driven fasteners are the most common defect we find on roofs that failed early. A photo-documented inspection will show you nail lines without anyone guessing.

Ventilation

An attic that runs 140 degrees in July bakes shingles from below. The code baseline is one square foot of net free vent area per 150 square feet of attic floor, or 1 per 300 with a balanced ridge-and-soffit layout. Roofs we tear off at 14 years almost always have blocked soffits, painted-over vents, or no ridge vent at all.

Slope and orientation

South and west faces take more UV and more hail. Low-slope sections hold water and snow longer. The same shingle can look 10 years older on the south slope than the north.

Trees and debris

Pine needles and cottonwood leaves hold moisture against shingles and dam gutters, which feeds ice dams in winter. Branches that touch the roof abrade granules every windy day.

Maintenance

Cleaning gutters, resealing exposed fasteners, replacing cracked pipe boots, and clearing debris from valleys are low-cost tasks that add years. A roof inspected every two to three years, and after every notable hail event, rarely surprises its owner.

sections.h2: How to tell where your roof is in its life
sections.html:
You do not need to climb a ladder to narrow it down. Start with these.

  1. Find the install date. Check the permit history with your city or county building department. Most Front Range jurisdictions keep re-roof permits searchable online. Your insurance declarations page or the original closing documents may also list it.
  2. Look at the gutters. A handful of granules after a storm is normal. Gutters full of them, or bald patches visible from the ground, mean the asphalt is exposed and failing.
  3. Walk the perimeter after wind. Lifted tabs, shingles in the yard, or exposed nail heads along the edges point to broken seals.
  4. Check the attic on a sunny day. Daylight at a penetration, rusty nail tips, dark staining on the underside of the decking, or compressed insulation below a valley are all water signs.
  5. Look at the flashing. Rust streaks below a chimney, cracked sealant at a pipe boot, or a wall flashing that has pulled away is often the real leak source on a roof that still has life in its shingles.
  6. Note the shape. Curling, cupping, or clawing shingles cannot be repaired. They have lost their flexibility and will not lie flat again.

If your roof is past 60 percent of the range in the table above and shows two or more of those signs, schedule an inspection before you have a claim to file. The free inspection we offer is written and photographed so you can take it to your agent or keep it for a future buyer.

sections.h2: Roof age and your insurance carrier
sections.html:
The practical lifespan of a roof in Colorado is increasingly set by underwriters, not weather. Carriers writing homeowners policies here have lost money on property lines in most recent years, and hail accounts for well over half of the premium dollar according to the state Division of Insurance. Their response has been to look hard at roof age.

  • Many carriers now decline new policies, or decline to renew, on composition roofs older than 15 to 20 years, or require a roof inspection before binding.
  • Others keep the policy but switch the roof to actual cash value once it passes an age threshold, often around 15 years. On a 15-year-old shingle roof with a 20-year expected life, that can mean a payout of a quarter of replacement cost, less the deductible.
  • Roof payment schedules pay a declining percentage by age and material. A 12-year-old composition roof might be scheduled at 60 percent.
  • Cosmetic damage exclusions, especially on metal, deny claims for hail that dents but does not cause leaks.

A new roof, particularly a Class 4 roof, resets that clock and usually earns a premium credit. Read the roof endorsement on your policy before you decide to squeeze another five years out of an aging roof. The savings can evaporate in one storm. Our guide to whether homeowners insurance covers roof replacement in Colorado goes deeper.

sections.h2: Repair or replace: a simple decision framework
sections.html:
Use these rules of thumb, then confirm with an inspection.

  • Repair when the roof is under two thirds of its expected life, damage is confined to one slope or one detail, and the shingles still lie flat and flex without cracking.
  • Replace when the roof is past 80 percent of its range, when repair costs approach a third of replacement, when there are already two layers, or when your carrier has moved it to actual cash value.
  • Upgrade when you are replacing anyway and plan to stay. The cost difference between a standard architectural shingle and a Class 4 shingle is modest relative to the whole job, and the step to standing seam metal buys 40 or more years and much lower hail exposure. We compare the math in our 30-year metal versus asphalt comparison.

Replacement cost varies by material, pitch, access, tear-off layers, and decking condition, so treat any number you see online as a starting point and ask for a written, itemized estimate. If a hail event is what prompted the question, document the roof first and read what to do after a hail storm before you sign anything.

faq.q: How long does an asphalt shingle roof last in Colorado?
faq.a: A 3-tab shingle roof typically lasts 15 to 20 years here, and an architectural shingle roof 20 to 30 years. Both numbers assume decent installation and attic ventilation. Hail, high-altitude UV, and wind along the foothills push most roofs toward the low end of those ranges, and a single severe hail event can end a roof at any age.

faq.q: Does a 30-year shingle really last 30 years in Colorado?
faq.a: Rarely. The 30-year figure is a warranty term, and most shingle warranties prorate heavily after the first decade. In Colorado, an architectural shingle sold as a 30-year product usually delivers 20 to 25 years of service before granule loss, brittleness, or hail makes replacement the better investment. Ventilation and slope orientation move that number several years in either direction.

faq.q: What is the longest-lasting roof for a Colorado home?
faq.a: Natural slate and clay tile last the longest, often 75 to 150 years or more, but both are heavy and expensive. For most homes, standing seam metal with a PVDF finish is the practical long-life choice at 40 to 70 years, with strong hail and wildfire performance. Synthetic slate and shake deliver 40 to 50 years at lower weight and cost.

faq.q: At what age will insurance companies stop covering my roof?
faq.a: There is no single statewide cutoff. Many Colorado carriers scrutinize composition roofs at 15 years and decline or non-renew somewhere between 15 and 20 years, or move the roof to actual cash value. Metal, tile, and Class 4 roofs are generally treated more generously. Check the roof endorsement on your own policy and ask your agent directly.

faq.q: How often should I have my roof inspected in Colorado?
faq.a: Every two to three years for a roof under 10 years old, annually once it passes 15, and after any hail event with stones of one inch or larger. Inspections are inexpensive compared with the interior damage a slow leak causes, and a written, photographed report gives you a dated record for your insurer and for a future home sale.

h1: Slate Roofing: Is It Worth It in Colorado?
title: Is Slate Roofing Worth It in CO
description: Is slate roofing worth it in Colorado? Cost per square, weight and structure, hail performance, and who should buy it. Get a free inspection.
excerpt: Slate is the longest-lived roof you can buy and the most demanding to install. This guide covers cost, weight, hail, and the structural questions to settle before you fall in love with the look.
intro:
A slate roof is the only roofing decision most people make once. Hard slate quarried in Vermont, Virginia, or Pennsylvania routinely outlasts the building under it, and a well-detailed slate roof on a Colorado home will still be shedding water when the third set of owners sells it. That longevity comes with weight, cost, and a short list of installers who know what they are doing. Whether it is worth it depends on the house, the budget, the hail exposure, and how long you intend to own the roof.

This guide gives you the numbers and the decision framework. For the service itself, see our slate roofing page.

sections.h2: What roofing slate is and where good slate comes from
sections.html:
Roofing slate is metamorphic rock split along its natural cleavage into thin, flat pieces, typically a quarter inch thick for standard roofs and up to three quarters of an inch or more for heavy textural roofs. It is fastened with copper or stainless nails through two pre-punched holes, laid with a headlap of three inches or more, and relies on gravity and overlap rather than sealant.

Slate quality is defined by ASTM C406, which grades stone by water absorption, weathering, and flexural strength:

  • S1: hard slate, expected service life of 75 years or more, water absorption of about a quarter of one percent. Virtually all new slate roofs in North America use S1 stone.
  • S2: softer slate, 40 to 75 years.
  • S3: soft slate, 20 to 40 years, rarely specified for roofing.

Source matters as much as grade. Vermont and New York produce dense, color-stable slates in green, gray, purple, and black. Virginia Buckingham and Pennsylvania Peach Bottom are famously hard black slates with service lives documented past 150 years. Pennsylvania soft-vein slates can fail in under 60 years. Some imported slate sold since the 1980s has shown delamination and rust staining in freeze-thaw climates, which is exactly the climate we have. The right way to buy slate is by quarry and grade, in writing, with the ASTM test report attached to the submittal.

sections.h2: Weight and structural requirements
sections.html:
Standard quarter-inch slate weighs roughly 800 to 1,000 pounds per square (100 square feet). Heavier textural and graduated roofs can reach 1,500 pounds per square or more. Compare that with about 250 pounds for an architectural shingle roof and 100 to 150 pounds for standing seam metal.

That difference is why slate is a structural project before it is a roofing project. Modern trusses are commonly designed for a dead load that assumes shingles. Adding 8 to 15 pounds per square foot of dead load on top of a Colorado snow load of 30 psf on the plains or 100 psf and up in the mountains can exceed what the framing was built for. Before anyone orders stone, you need:

  • A review of rafter or truss size, span, and spacing, and of the decking thickness.
  • A structural engineer's letter where the numbers are close, which the building department will usually require on a re-roof that changes the covering weight.
  • A plan for the bearing path: slate load has to get to the foundation, not just the rafters.

On a new custom home, slate is easy to design for. On a 1970s ranch in Fort Collins with 2x6 rafters at 24 inches, it may require sistering or new purlins, and that cost belongs in the decision. If the framing cannot carry it, Class 4 synthetic slate keeps the look at a fraction of the weight.

sections.h2: Slate and Colorado hail
sections.html:
This is the question that decides most Front Range slate projects. The honest answer has three parts.

Hard, thick slate resists most hail. A three-eighths or half-inch S1 slate shrugs off the one-inch hail that shreds asphalt shingles. Hail large enough to crack it is rare, and when it happens the damage is to individual slates, which are replaced one at a time rather than as a whole roof.

Thin and soft slate is vulnerable. Quarter-inch stone, and anything below S1, can crack under hail of two inches or larger, which Larimer and Weld counties see every few years. Cracked slates let water in at the nail holes and are easy to miss from the ground.

Insurance treats slate differently. Some carriers will not write replacement cost on a slate roof, or will require a specialty appraisal. Others apply cosmetic exclusions. Ask before you buy, and keep the quarry documentation, because a claim on a slate roof is an argument about what the slate was.

Where hail is the main risk, as it is in Greeley or along the I-25 corridor, we usually show clients heavy S1 slate alongside synthetic slate and stone-coated steel and lay out the tradeoffs. In the foothills and mountains, where wildfire and snow matter more than hail, natural slate makes a stronger case. See our guide on spotting hail damage for what to look for after a storm on any roof.

sections.h2: What slate costs in Colorado
sections.html:
Slate is the most expensive roof covering installed on homes. National installed pricing published by roofing cost guides runs roughly as follows, and Colorado labor, steep pitches, and mountain access push toward the upper end:

SystemTypical installed cost per squareTypical service life
Hard S1 slate, standard quarter inch$2,200 to $2,80075 to 100 years or more
Hard S1 slate, three-eighths to half inch$2,800 to $3,500100 years or more
Hard S1 slate, heavy or graduated$3,500 to $4,500150 years or more
Soft S2 slate$1,600 to $2,00040 to 75 years
Synthetic polymer slate (Class 4)$1,100 to $1,60040 to 50 years
Architectural asphalt shingle$450 to $75020 to 30 years

Those figures vary by pitch, complexity, access, tear-off, and whether structural work is needed. Roofs above 8/12 can cost up to half again as much to install. Copper flashings, snow retention, and engineering are usually separate line items. On a 30-square home, a quality slate roof is a six-figure project, and we say that plainly so no one is surprised at the estimate stage. Financing is available for specialty roofs, and a written itemized estimate will show you exactly where the money goes.

sections.h2: The details that make or break a slate roof
sections.html:
Slate roofs do not fail because the stone wears out. They fail because something cheaper under or around the stone gave up first. Specify these and you will get the century roof you paid for.

  • Copper or stainless flashings. Valleys, step flashing, chimney saddles, and wall counterflashing should be 16-ounce copper or stainless steel. Galvanized steel rusts out in 25 to 40 years, and replacing it means disturbing sound slate.
  • Copper or stainless nails. Electro-galvanized nails are the most common cause of slate roofs shedding slates at 50 to 70 years. The stone is fine; the nails are gone.
  • Correct headlap and exposure. Three inches of headlap minimum on pitches above 8/12, four inches on lower pitches. Short headlap is an invitation for wind-driven snow.
  • Solid decking. Slate wants solid wood boards or a thick plywood deck, not thin OSB, and the nails must be driven to hang the slate, not pinned tight.
  • High-temperature underlayment. A self-adhered ice barrier at eaves, valleys, and penetrations, with a durable synthetic or felt underlayment across the field. The underlayment is a secondary layer, not the roof, but it needs to outlast the nails.
  • Snow retention. In the mountains, slate sheds snow in sheets. Engineered snow guards protect people, decks, and gutters.

All of this is why slate installers are few. Walking a slate roof wrong breaks slate. The people doing it should be able to show you a slate ripper, slate hooks, and photos of their last three jobs.

sections.h2: Repair and maintenance over a century
sections.html:
A slate roof needs an inspection every few years and after large hail. Expect to replace a few cracked or slipped slates per decade. A single slate is removed with a ripper that cuts the nails, and the replacement is secured with a copper slate hook or a copper bib, with no visible fastener and no sealant. Done correctly, the repair is as permanent as the roof.

Between years 50 and 80, plan on a flashing campaign: valleys, chimney flashings, and any galvanized metal get replaced in copper. If the original roof used steel nails, a lift-and-relay on new underlayment with copper nails can reuse most of the original stone and reset the clock for another century. That is a smaller job than it sounds and far cheaper than new slate.

Moss and lichen are rarely a problem in Colorado's dry air. Never pressure wash slate, and never let a gutter installer or satellite technician walk the field unsupervised. Our roof repair team handles individual slate replacement and flashing work on existing roofs as well as new installations.

sections.h2: So, is it worth it? A decision framework
sections.html:
Slate is worth it when most of these are true:

  • The house is a long-term hold, a legacy property, or a custom build designed around it.
  • The structure can carry the load, or the cost to make it carry the load is acceptable.
  • The home's value supports a six-figure roof, and the architecture benefits from the material.
  • You are in a foothills or mountain setting where fire resistance and snow performance matter and giant hail is less frequent.
  • You want a roof that will not be replaced in your lifetime and that appraisers and buyers recognize as a premium asset.

Slate is probably not worth it when:

  • You expect to sell in under 10 years; a metal roof or synthetic slate returns more of its cost.
  • The framing is marginal and engineering adds tens of thousands.
  • Your location sees frequent two-inch hail and your insurer will not write replacement cost on slate.
  • The budget forces thin or soft slate. A quarter-inch S2 roof is a worse value than a good synthetic.

Start with a free, photo-documented inspection and a structural read of the framing. We will tell you in writing whether slate fits the house, and show you the alternatives side by side.

faq.q: How much does a slate roof cost in Colorado?
faq.a: Installed hard S1 slate typically runs $2,200 to $4,500 per square depending on thickness, with heavy and graduated roofs at the top of that range. Steep pitches, mountain access, copper flashings, structural upgrades, and tear-off add to the total. Costs vary by home, so treat those figures as a planning range and ask for a written itemized estimate.

faq.q: Can my existing house support a slate roof?
faq.a: Many can, but it must be checked. Slate adds roughly 8 to 15 pounds per square foot of dead load, several times the weight of shingles. We review rafter size, span, spacing, and decking, and involve a structural engineer when the numbers are close or when the building department requires a letter. If the structure falls short, synthetic slate is the usual alternative.

faq.q: How does slate hold up to hail?
faq.a: Thick, hard S1 slate resists most Colorado hail, and hail large enough to crack it damages individual slates rather than the whole roof. Thin quarter-inch stone and softer grades are more vulnerable to two-inch and larger hail. Carriers sometimes limit coverage on slate, so confirm your policy terms before buying and keep the quarry and grade documentation.

faq.q: How long does a slate roof last?
faq.a: Hard S1 slate from quarries in Vermont, Virginia, and Pennsylvania routinely lasts 75 to 150 years or more. The roof usually fails at the nails and flashings long before the stone, which is why copper or stainless fasteners and flashings matter. Soft S2 slate lasts 40 to 75 years, and imported slate of unknown grade can fail much sooner in freeze-thaw climates.

faq.q: What is the difference between natural slate and synthetic slate?
faq.a: Natural slate is split stone weighing 800 to 1,500 pounds per square with a service life measured in generations. Synthetic slate is a molded polymer product weighing a quarter as much, typically rated Class 4 for impact and Class A for fire, lasting 40 to 50 years at roughly a third to half the installed cost. Synthetic needs no structural upgrade on most homes.

h1: Roof Coatings for Flat Commercial Roofs in Colorado
title: Flat Roof Coatings Colorado
description: Flat roof coatings for Colorado commercial roofs: silicone vs acrylic, moisture surveys, cost per square foot, and when to say no. Get a free inspection.
keywords: roof coating cost per square foot
excerpt: A coating can add 10 to 20 years to a sound flat roof for a fraction of replacement cost. It can also waste every dollar on the wrong roof. Here is how to tell which roof you have.
intro:
Fluid-applied roof coatings are the best value in commercial roofing when the roof underneath qualifies, and the most expensive paint job in the building's history when it does not. Property managers and building owners in Northern Colorado get pitched coatings constantly, often by crews that never cut a core sample or pulled an adhesion test. This guide explains what a coating actually does, how the four main chemistries differ, how a roof is qualified, what it should cost, and the specific conditions under which you should say no.

For how we approach the work, see our roof coatings service page.

sections.h2: What a roof coating is, and what it is not
sections.html:
A roof coating is a liquid elastomeric membrane, sprayed or rolled over an existing low-slope roof, that cures into a seamless waterproof film 20 to 40 mils thick. It bonds to TPO, EPDM, modified bitumen, built-up roofing, metal, and spray foam. Seams, penetrations, curbs, and drains are reinforced first with fabric or mastic, then the field coat goes on.

What it does: seals aged seams and pinholes, stops UV degradation of the membrane beneath, reflects solar load, and restores a roof that is structurally sound but worn. Done to a manufacturer's inspected specification, it carries a 10 to 20 year material and labor warranty and can be recoated at the end of that term with no tear-off.

What it does not do: add R-value, dry out wet insulation, bridge open seams or failed flashings, fix ponding caused by bad drainage, or rescue a membrane at the end of its life. It is also not for shingle roofs, no matter who tells you otherwise. A coating is a restoration, not a replacement, and the distinction decides whether you get 15 years or 15 months.

sections.h2: Silicone, acrylic, urethane, and SEBS compared
sections.html:
Four chemistries cover nearly every commercial coating job. Each has a roof it is right for.

In practice, silicone is the default for Colorado flat roofs because so many of them pond somewhere. Acrylic earns its place on metal and on roofs with real slope, where its lower cost and easy recoat shine. Urethane shows up as a tough base coat under silicone on roofs with mechanical traffic or hail exposure, which is most of Weld and Larimer counties. SEBS is a metal-roof specialist.

sections.h2: Qualifying the roof: moisture survey and adhesion testing
sections.html:
No one should quote a coating without two tests, and both should be in the proposal.

Moisture survey

Wet insulation under a coating stays wet forever. It rots the deck, grows mold, kills R-value, and blisters the coating off from below. A moisture survey finds it before the coating hides it. Methods include infrared thermography at dusk, when wet insulation holds heat longer than dry, nuclear or capacitance meters, and core cuts that physically confirm what the scan shows. The survey produces a map. Wet areas are cut out and replaced with new insulation and membrane patches before anything is coated.

A common rule in the industry is that once roughly 25 percent of the insulation is wet, replacement beats restoration. The exact threshold depends on the cost of the wet-area repairs relative to a new roof, which is why we quote both.

Adhesion testing

Coatings fail at the bond line. Field adhesion tests follow the manufacturer's protocol, usually a version of the ASTM D903 peel test or a simple cross-hatch test: the coating is applied to small test patches on each substrate type, cured, and pulled. If it does not reach the specified pull strength, the surface needs a different primer, more aggressive cleaning, or a different chemistry. Aged TPO, in particular, can be difficult to bond to without primer. Chalked acrylic and silicone-over-anything-but-silicone are other common failures.

Add to those two tests a pull test on fasteners for metal roofs, a seam probe across the whole roof for single-ply, and a drainage check with a hose if the roof is dry. Our commercial roofing proposals include all of it in writing with photographs.

sections.h2: Altitude, UV, and cool-roof performance in Colorado
sections.html:
Solar load is the hidden roof killer at 5,000 feet and above. Thin air lets more ultraviolet through, and more than 300 sunny days a year means the membrane is under UV attack most of the time. UV breaks the polymer chains in TPO and EPDM, chalks acrylics, and drives the thermal cycling that fatigues seams. A dark roof on a 90-degree July afternoon in Loveland can reach 150 degrees or more at the surface.

A white reflective coating changes that. Published cool-roof data from manufacturers and federal energy programs put initial solar reflectance for white silicone and acrylic at roughly 80 to 90 percent, with surface temperatures held within a few degrees of ambient. That delivers three things:

  • Lower cooling demand, often cited as a 10 to 15 percent reduction in peak cooling load on single-story buildings with roof-dominated heat gain. Actual savings depend on insulation, HVAC, and occupancy, so treat any dollar figure as an estimate.
  • Less thermal cycling, which is what makes seams and flashings last longer under the coating.
  • Longer coating life, because the film itself runs cooler.

Two Colorado caveats: reflectivity drops as dirt accumulates, and silicone holds dirt more than acrylic, so plan on a rinse every couple of years. And in a heating-dominated climate, a white roof gives up a little winter solar gain. On an insulated commercial roof, the summer savings outweigh that, but on a poorly insulated building it is worth running the numbers.

sections.h2: What a coating costs and what the warranty should say
sections.html:
Installed coating costs vary with chemistry, thickness, substrate prep, and how much wet material has to be replaced first. Typical Colorado ranges for a complete system, including cleaning, seam reinforcement, and the specified film thickness:

SystemTypical installed cost per square foot
Acrylic, two coats with primer$1.50 to $3.00
Silicone, high-solids single or two coat$2.50 to $4.50
Urethane base plus silicone top$3.50 to $5.50
Wet-area replacement (insulation and membrane patch)$8 to $15 per square foot of wet area
Tear-off and new single-ply membrane, for comparison$8 to $14

Those are planning figures, not quotes; every roof is priced from its own survey. The warranty is where you separate real systems from paint. Ask for:

  • A manufacturer system warranty with labor and material coverage, 10, 15, or 20 years, issued only after a manufacturer or third-party inspection of the finished roof. A material-only warranty means the manufacturer will send you buckets if it fails.
  • The specified dry film thickness in mils, by coat, in the contract, and wet-mil readings during application. Warranty length tracks thickness.
  • A contractor workmanship warranty that covers seams, penetrations, and flashings, where coating jobs actually leak.
  • Terms for recoating at the end of the term, which is where a coating earns its value a second time.
  • Exclusions, especially for ponding (on acrylic), hail, and foot traffic, and what maintenance the warranty requires.

Our warranty page explains what to ask for on any roofing system.

sections.h2: When a coating is the wrong call
sections.html:
Say no to a coating, or at least pause, when any of these are true:

  • The moisture survey shows widespread wet insulation. Past roughly a quarter of the roof, replacement wins.
  • Seams are opening or the membrane is shrinking. EPDM that has pulled away from walls and curbs needs mechanical repair, not a film.
  • The deck is damaged. Rusted metal deck, rotted wood deck, or ponding that has deflected the structure are not coating problems.
  • The roof ponds and someone is proposing acrylic. Fix the drainage or specify silicone.
  • There are already two or more roof systems stacked. Code may require tear-off, and the weight is already a concern.
  • The pitch is steep. Above roughly 3/12, coatings become a slip hazard and other systems make more sense.
  • No one has tested adhesion. A proposal without a pull test is a guess with your money.
  • It is a shingle roof. Coating shingles voids warranties, traps moisture, and does not work.

A contractor who does restoration and replacement will tell you which one you need. One who only sells coatings will find a coating.

sections.h2: Questions to ask before you sign
sections.html:
1. Will you perform a moisture survey and provide the map? What method?
  2. Which chemistry, which manufacturer, which product, and why for this roof?
  3. What dry film thickness is specified, and how will you verify it?
  4. How are seams, drains, curbs, and penetrations reinforced before the field coat?
  5. Who issues the warranty, who inspects before it is issued, and does it cover labor?
  6. What is the price to replace wet areas, per square foot, if the survey finds more than expected?
  7. What is the replacement price for the same roof, so I can compare?
  8. What is the recoat plan and cost at the end of the warranty?
  9. What is the fall protection and safety plan, and will tenants be affected?

Get those answers in writing and the decision usually makes itself. If you own or manage a flat roof in Northern Colorado and want a coat-or-replace recommendation you can take to an owner or a board, start with a free inspection. The report includes photographs, a drainage assessment, and both numbers.

faq.q: How much does a commercial roof coating cost in Colorado?
faq.a: Installed systems typically run $1.50 to $3.00 per square foot for acrylic, $2.50 to $4.50 for silicone, and $3.50 to $5.50 for a urethane and silicone combination, plus wet-area replacement where the moisture survey finds it. A tear-off and new membrane generally costs $8 to $14 per square foot. Actual pricing varies by roof condition, size, and access.

faq.q: Which is better, silicone or acrylic roof coating?
faq.a: Silicone is better wherever water ponds, because it cures by moisture and does not soften under standing water. It also resists UV without chalking. Acrylic is cheaper, easier to recoat, and performs well on metal and sloped roofs with positive drainage, but it fails under ponding. The right answer depends on your roof’s drainage, substrate, and budget.

faq.q: Can a roof coating fix leaks on my flat roof?
faq.a: Yes, when the leaks come from aged seams, pinholes, and flashing fatigue on a roof whose insulation and deck are still sound. No, when the insulation is saturated, the deck is damaged, or the membrane is shrinking away from walls. A moisture survey and seam probe tell the difference, and the wet areas have to be replaced before coating.

faq.q: How long does a roof coating last?
faq.a: Manufacturer system warranties run 10 to 20 years depending on chemistry and film thickness. Silicone systems at higher mil thicknesses carry the longest terms. At the end of the warranty, most systems can be cleaned and recoated without a tear-off, which is where coatings earn their value a second time. Regular inspection and keeping drains clear extend the term.

faq.q: Does a white roof coating save energy in Colorado?
faq.a: Yes, in summer. A white silicone or acrylic coating reflects most of the high-altitude solar load and keeps roof surface temperatures far below a dark membrane, which lowers cooling demand and reduces the thermal cycling that wears out seams. Winter heating gain is slightly reduced, but on an insulated commercial roof the net effect is positive. Actual savings depend on the building.

h1: Mountain Home Roofing: Snow Load, Ice Dams, and What Works at 8,000 Feet
title: Mountain Roofing Snow Load Guide
description: Mountain roofing in Colorado: snow loads by town, ice dam physics, cold roofs, ice and water shield, snow retention, Class A. Get a free inspection.
excerpt: Above 8,000 feet a roof is a snow, ice, wind, and fire problem before it is a water problem. Here are the numbers, the physics, and the assemblies that survive Colorado winters.
intro:
A roof that would last 25 years in Loveland can fail in five in Breckenridge. Not because the material is different, but because the loads are. A mountain roof carries snow measured in the hundreds of pounds per square foot, sheds it in avalanches onto decks and doorways, fights ice dams fed by every bit of heat the house leaks, and must do all of it while meeting wildfire code in a wildland urban interface. The details that are optional at 5,000 feet are mandatory at 8,000.

This guide covers what changes with elevation, the snow load numbers for the towns we serve, how ice dams form and how to stop them, what cold-roof and warm-roof assemblies mean, how to choose and detail metal, and where heat cable actually belongs. For the service overview, see Breckenridge, Vail, Steamboat Springs, and Estes Park.

sections.h2: What changes above 7,000 feet
sections.html:
• Snow stays. On the plains, snow melts in days. In Summit and Routt counties it accumulates from November to April, and the roof carries the season's total minus whatever slides off.
  • Everything slides. A metal roof at 6/12 or steeper releases its snow in a single sheet when the sun hits it. Without retention, that sheet lands on whatever is below.
  • Ice dams are the default. Long nights, deep snow, and houses full of heat make eave ice a given unless the assembly is designed against it.
  • Wind is engineered. Ridge-top lots in Eagle and Grand counties see ultimate design wind speeds of 115 to 140 miles per hour and up, and uplift at eaves and corners is the design driver for fastening.
  • Fire is code. Most mountain jurisdictions require Class A roof assemblies, prohibit wood shakes, and the 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code extends those rules statewide to mapped WUI zones, with re-roofs of 25 percent or more of the roof triggering compliance.
  • The season is short. Reliable roofing weather runs roughly June through October. Permits, design review, and material lead times have to be lined up by spring.

sections.h2: Snow load numbers by town
sections.html:
Ground snow load is set by the county or town and increases with elevation. Roof snow load is derived from it using exposure, slope, and thermal factors, and both appear on the structural sheet of any permitted re-roof that changes weight. The table below gives the published design values and typical roof loads for the areas we serve. Verify the number for a specific parcel with the building department before designing anything.

Summit, Eagle, Grand, and Routt counties use site-specific maps, and Steamboat is among the heaviest in the state. Those loads are why slate, concrete tile, and even a second layer of shingles need an engineer's sign-off in the mountains, and why drifting against dormers and lower roofs, which can double the local load, must be designed, not ignored.

sections.h2: How ice dams form, and why they are a heat problem
sections.html:
An ice dam forms when the upper roof surface is above freezing and the eave is below it. Snow melts on the warm part of the roof, runs down under the snowpack, and refreezes at the cold overhang. The ridge of ice grows, water pools behind it, and the pool works back up the roof under the shingles or panel laps and into the wall.

What makes the upper roof warm is heat from the house. A foot of snow is roughly R-10 to R-15 of insulation, so even on a 10-degree night the roof deck under deep snow can sit above 32 degrees if the attic is leaking heat. The three leak paths are:

  1. Air leakage through recessed lights, plumbing and wiring penetrations, attic hatches, and top plates. This is the biggest one and the cheapest to fix.
  2. Conduction through thin insulation, especially at the eaves where trusses pinch the depth to a few inches.
  3. Ductwork and equipment in the attic, which should not be there in a mountain house.

Icicles are the warning sign. A roof with no icicles is a cold roof. A roof with a row of them has a heat problem, and the dam is already forming behind them. Roofing alone cannot fix this. Ice and water shield keeps the leak out of the house; it does not stop the dam.

sections.h2: Cold roof versus warm roof
sections.html:
Mountain roofs are designed one of two ways.

Cold (vented) roof

The roof deck is kept at outdoor temperature by a continuous air channel from soffit to ridge beneath it. In a vented attic, that means an airtight ceiling plane, deep insulation (R-49 to R-60 in Climate Zone 7), raised-heel trusses so the insulation stays thick at the eaves, and balanced soffit and ridge vents with a clear air path at every rafter bay. On a cathedral ceiling, the channel runs between the insulation and the deck. Federal building science guidance calls for a two-inch air space where ground snow exceeds 30 psf.

Warm (unvented) roof

Insulation sits directly against or above the deck with no air channel, usually closed-cell spray foam below or rigid insulation above. It works where the air barrier is perfect and the insulation is thick enough that the deck never warms. In heavy-snow country, the recommended practice is to add a vented over-roof: a second deck on sleepers above the insulated one, with air moving beneath it. That is the hybrid many Summit County custom homes use.

The rule of thumb for an existing house: fix the ceiling air barrier first, add insulation second, verify ventilation third, and only then talk about the roof covering. A new roof over a leaking ceiling will ice dam on its first winter.

sections.h2: Underlayment and ice barrier: full coverage is the mountain standard
sections.html:
The International Residential Code, section R905.1.2, requires an ice barrier of self-adhered polymer-modified bitumen from the eave to at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line in areas with a history of ice damming. That 24 inches is measured horizontally, so on a 12-inch overhang and 8/12 pitch the membrane has to run about 50 inches up the slope, which is more than one roll width.

Mountain jurisdictions go further. The Town of Breckenridge, for one, requires complete coverage of self-adhering ice and water shield over the entire roof deck, verified at an underlayment inspection, and high-temperature membrane under any metal roof. Many other towns above 7,000 feet, and most architects, specify the same. The reasons are practical: wind-driven snow finds every lap, meltwater travels sideways under a snowpack, and the underlayment is the only thing standing between a slid panel seam and the ceiling.

Specify a high-temperature self-adhered membrane rated to 240 degrees or more under metal, because a dark metal roof in June sun will cook a standard membrane into the panels. Ask for valley metal and drip edge in the underlayment inspection photos. If a proposal says ice and water shield at eaves and valleys only, it was written for the Front Range.

sections.h2: Metal roofs and snow retention
sections.html:
Standing seam metal is the default mountain roof for good reasons: it is Class A, sheds snow rather than holding it, handles freeze-thaw without absorbing water, and lasts 40 to 70 years. Mechanically seamed panels with concealed clips allow the panel to expand and contract and resist the uplift that ridge-top wind produces. Exposed-fastener panels, by contrast, have thousands of gasketed screws that loosen through thermal cycling and leak within a decade at altitude.

The catch is that a slick metal roof releases its snow all at once. A roof avalanche can crush a deck rail, bury a doorway, shear off a gas meter, or injure someone below. Snow retention is therefore part of the roof design, not an accessory:

  • Continuous rail or fence systems hold the whole slope and are the standard for occupied areas below the eave.
  • Pad-style guards in a staggered field pattern break the slab into smaller releases and suit lighter loads.
  • Clamp-to-seam attachment grips the standing seam without penetrating the panel, preserving the warranty. Screw-through guards on a standing seam roof are a leak waiting to happen.
  • Engineered layout. Manufacturers calculate rows and spacing from the roof snow load, pitch, panel profile, and eave-to-ridge length. A 100 psf roof at 8/12 may need two or three rows. Ask for the layout drawing and the attachment pull-test values.

Snow retention also protects gutters, which should be heavy-gauge, bracketed every 24 inches, and often heated on the north side. Many mountain homes skip gutters entirely and manage drip lines with drainage at grade.

sections.h2: Heat cable realities
sections.html:
Self-regulating heat cable zigzagged along the eaves and run through the gutters and downspouts does one thing: it melts channels through the ice so meltwater can escape. It does not stop the dam from forming, it costs real money to run all winter, it fails after 5 to 10 years of UV and abrasion, and it is the first thing a sliding snow slab tears off.

It belongs on a roof as a last resort, where geometry leaves no alternative: a north-facing valley that dumps onto an entry, a low-slope section below a tall wall, or a historic house that cannot be re-insulated. Even then, it should be paired with snow retention above it and installed with a dedicated circuit and a thermostat or moisture sensor so it is not running on dry days. If a contractor proposes heat cable as the first fix on a new roof, the house has an air sealing and insulation problem that cable will only hide.

sections.h2: Class A roofs and wildfire at altitude
sections.html:
Every mountain town we serve sits in or near the wildland urban interface. Summit County, Pitkin County, Boulder County, and many municipalities already prohibit wood shakes and require Class A roof assemblies. The 2025 Colorado Wildfire Resiliency Code applies to mapped zones statewide, and a re-roof of 25 percent or more of the surface triggers it, along with ember-resistant vents and non-combustible gutters.

Standing seam metal, concrete and clay tile, natural slate, and Class A synthetic shake all qualify. The roof covering is only part of the assembly: the underlayment, deck, and the gaps at eaves, ridges, and vents all matter to a Class A rating. Ember-resistant vents, boxed-in eaves, metal drip edge, and screened gutters keep burning debris out of the attic. Our guide to roofing materials for Colorado wildfire zones compares the assemblies in detail.
