Whatever the covering, a mountain roof succeeds or fails on the details: the air barrier under it, the underlayment on it, the snow retention attached to it, and the schedule that gets it done before the first storm. Start with a free inspection and a written scope that names every one of those.

faq.q: What is the roof snow load in Breckenridge or Vail?
faq.a: Both Summit and Eagle counties use site-specific snow load maps rather than a single number. Published design values for Breckenridge and Vail area homes commonly land at roof snow loads of 75 to 100 pounds per square foot and higher, with drift and sliding loads on top. The building department confirms the figure for a given parcel, and any re-roof that changes weight needs it on the structural sheet.

faq.q: How do I stop ice dams on my mountain home?
faq.a: In order: seal the ceiling air barrier at every penetration, add insulation to Climate Zone 7 levels with full depth at the eaves, and verify soffit-to-ridge ventilation so the deck stays cold. Then install full-coverage self-adhered ice and water shield as the backstop. Heat cable is the last resort for geometry that cannot be fixed, not the first step.

faq.q: Do I need ice and water shield over the whole roof above 7,000 feet?
faq.a: The IRC minimum is 24 inches inside the exterior wall line, but most mountain jurisdictions and architects require or specify full-deck coverage, and towns such as Breckenridge mandate it and inspect for it. Under metal, the membrane must be a high-temperature grade. Given wind-driven snow and sideways meltwater travel, full coverage is the sensible standard at altitude regardless of local code.

faq.q: Are snow guards required on a metal roof in Colorado?
faq.a: Not by statewide code, but many mountain towns require them where roofs shed onto walkways, entries, decks, utilities, or neighboring property, and design review boards ask for the layout. Beyond code, they are a safety and liability issue. The layout should be engineered from the roof snow load, pitch, and panel profile, and clamp to the seam without penetrating the panel.

faq.q: What is the best roof for a Colorado mountain home?
faq.a: For most homes, mechanically seamed standing seam metal with a PVDF finish, engineered snow retention, and full high-temperature ice and water shield. It is Class A, sheds snow, resists wind uplift, and lasts 40 to 70 years. Class A synthetic shake is the alternative where a cedar look is wanted, and slate or tile suit custom homes engineered to carry them.

h1: How to Read a Roofing Estimate (Line by Line)
title: How to Read a Roofing Estimate
description: How to read a roofing estimate line by line: squares, waste, tear-off, decking, flashing, O&P, and Colorado contract rules. Get a free inspection.
keywords: how to read a roofing estimate
excerpt: Three estimates for the same roof can differ by thousands of dollars and still all be honest. Here is what every line means, what should be on it, and what Colorado law requires in the contract.
intro:
A roofing estimate is a technical document written by people who read dozens of them a week, handed to someone who may read one in a lifetime. The gap is where bad decisions happen. A low bid that leaves out decking, ice barrier, and permit fees is not low; it is incomplete, and the difference shows up as a change order the day the old roof comes off.

This guide walks through a residential roofing estimate from the header to the signature line, in roughly the order the work happens. It covers the Xactimate-style line items an insurance claim produces, the quantities and waste factors behind them, what "per code" should actually mean, and the contract terms Colorado law requires. Use it to compare bids on the same scope, which is the only comparison that means anything.

sections.h2: The header and the scope statement
sections.html:
Before the numbers, check the top of the page.

  • Legal business name, physical address, and phone. A post office box or a cell number alone is a warning sign in a hail year, when out-of-state crews follow the storms.
  • Insurance. Colorado requires residential roofing contracts to identify the contractor's liability insurer and surety, if any, with contact information. Ask for a certificate of insurance naming you as certificate holder, showing general liability and workers' compensation. A roofer without workers' comp puts the injury claim on your homeowners policy.
  • Property address and roof description. Pitch, number of stories, and the roof sections included. Detached garages and sheds should be listed or explicitly excluded.
  • Scope statement. One paragraph that says what is being done: full tear-off to the deck, replacement with a named shingle or panel, and the components below. "Re-roof per code" is not a scope.
  • Approximate start and completion dates. Required in Colorado contracts.

Every estimate we issue is written and itemized, and the roof replacement scope names every product by manufacturer and model.

sections.h2: Measurements, squares, and waste factor
sections.html:
Roofing is sold by the square, which is 100 square feet of roof surface. A 2,000 square foot ranch with a 6/12 pitch and overhangs has roughly 24 to 26 squares of roof, not 20. The estimate should show the measured area and the source: an aerial measurement report, a hand measurement, or the insurance adjuster's sketch.

Waste factor accounts for cuts at hips, valleys, ridges, and edges. Typical waste is 10 percent on a simple gable roof and 15 percent or more on a cut-up hip roof with dormers. Insurance estimating software applies waste as a percentage line below the shingle quantity. Two things to check:

  • The waste percentage matches the roof shape. Ten percent on a complex hip roof means the crew will run short or substitute.
  • Waste is applied to field shingles, not to starter, ridge cap, or underlayment, which have their own quantities in linear feet or rolls.

If two estimates show different square counts for the same roof, ask each contractor how they measured. A difference of two squares at $500 to $700 per square installed explains a lot of bid spreads.

sections.h2: Tear-off, layers, and decking
sections.html:
Tear-off is priced per square per layer. Many Front Range homes built before 2000 have two layers, and the estimate should state how many it includes. Colorado jurisdictions following the IRC allow a maximum of two layers, so a roof with two already must be torn off completely. If the number of layers is unknown, the estimate should say what the second layer will cost if found.

Decking is the sheathing under the roof, usually 7/16 inch OSB or half inch plywood on newer homes and 1x skip boards or plank on older ones. No one knows its condition until the shingles are off. A good estimate handles this one of two ways:

  • A unit price per 4x8 sheet for replacement, typically in the range of $75 to $150 installed depending on material and access, applied only to sheets that are rotted, delaminated, or broken.
  • An allowance of a set number of sheets, with the unit price for anything beyond it.

Skip-sheathed roofs going to shingles need a full re-deck, which is a separate and significant line. Ask to be called and shown photos before any decking beyond the allowance is replaced. Our crews photograph every sheet.

Haul-off and dump fees cover the dumpster and landfill charges, which run several hundred dollars and scale with layers. An estimate that omits disposal is not complete.

sections.h2: Underlayment, ice barrier, starter, and drip edge
sections.html:
These are the lines most often cut from a low bid, and they are the ones that keep water out when a shingle fails.

  • Ice and water shield is a self-adhered membrane at eaves, valleys, around penetrations, and along walls. The IRC requires it at eaves to 24 inches inside the exterior wall line where ice dams occur, which covers the entire Front Range and all mountain towns. Many mountain jurisdictions require full coverage. The estimate should state where it goes and in what quantity, in squares or rolls.
  • Synthetic underlayment covers the rest of the deck. Synthetic has largely replaced 15 and 30 pound felt because it does not wrinkle, tear, or absorb water. The line should name the product.
  • Starter strip runs along eaves and rakes under the first course, with a factory adhesive that seals the edge against wind. Cut-up field shingles used as starter are a shortcut that fails in Front Range wind. Priced in linear feet.
  • Drip edge is the metal flashing at eaves and rakes that directs water into the gutter and off the fascia. Required by the IRC on shingle roofs. Priced in linear feet, with color and gauge noted.

When an estimate says "per code" for any of these, ask which code edition the jurisdiction has adopted and what that requires. In most Northern Colorado cities it means the 2021 IRC with local amendments. Per code is a floor, not a specification.

sections.h2: Shingles, ridge cap, and ventilation
sections.html:
The field shingle line should name the manufacturer, product line, and color, and state the impact rating if any. A Class 4 shingle under UL 2218 is a different product at a different price from the standard architectural shingle in the same line, and it is what earns the insurance discount. "Architectural shingle, 30 year" tells you nothing.

Hip and ridge cap is a separate, thicker shingle made for ridges, priced per linear foot. Field shingles cut into caps crack in cold weather. On a Class 4 roof the cap should be Class 4 as well, or the rating is not whole.

Ventilation appears as ridge vent in linear feet, or as box vents or turbines by the each. The estimate should also account for intake at the soffits, because exhaust without intake does nothing. Manufacturers condition their shingle warranties on adequate ventilation, so an estimate that reuses an old, inadequate vent layout can quietly void coverage.

sections.h2: Flashing, penetrations, and accessories
sections.html:
Roofs leak at the transitions, not in the field. Each of these should be a line or an explicit note.

  • Pipe boots at every plumbing vent, by the each. Rubber boots crack in Colorado UV in 8 to 12 years; lead or metal boots with a rubber collar last longer.
  • Step flashing where the roof meets a wall, one piece per course, priced in linear feet. It should be new, not reused.
  • Counterflashing at chimneys and walls, cut into the masonry or tucked behind siding, in linear feet.
  • Chimney flashing including a cricket or saddle on the upslope side of any chimney wider than 30 inches, which the IRC requires.
  • Valley metal where valleys are open, or a note that valleys are closed-cut over ice barrier.
  • Furnace and water heater vents, satellite dish removal and reset, skylight flashing kits, and gutter detach and reset as applicable.

Reused flashing is the most common hidden saving in a low bid. It is also where the roof leaks in year three. If a line says "flashing as needed," ask for the quantity and the material.

sections.h2: Permits, fees, and overhead and profit
sections.html:
Permit: a re-roof permit is required in every Northern Colorado jurisdiction, and the fee should be its own line. The permit gets you a mid-roof or final inspection by the city or county, which is your independent check on the work. A contractor who suggests skipping the permit is suggesting you skip the inspection.

Overhead and profit (O&P) appears on insurance estimates as a percentage, commonly 10 percent overhead plus 10 percent profit, applied when the job involves multiple trades or enough complexity that a general contractor's coordination is warranted. On a retail estimate, overhead and profit are usually built into unit prices rather than listed separately. Either is legitimate; what matters is that you are not paying it twice.

Depreciation on an insurance claim is not a contractor line, but it affects what you pay. The carrier's estimate shows replacement cost value, deducts depreciation to reach actual cash value, and pays the first check at ACV. The recoverable depreciation is released after the work is complete and invoiced. Your out-of-pocket cost is your deductible, plus any upgrades you choose. See our guide to how homeowners insurance pays for a roof in Colorado.

sections.h2: Payment terms and what Colorado law requires
sections.html:
Colorado's residential roofing statute, C.R.S. 6-22-101 and following, sets contract terms every homeowner should know.

  • Written contract with scope, materials, cost, approximate dates, contractor contact information, insurer and surety information, and the contractor's deposit and cancellation policy.
  • 72-hour right to cancel. You may rescind the contract within 72 hours of signing and receive a full refund of any deposit.
  • Right to cancel after a claim denial. If the work is to be paid by insurance and the carrier denies the claim in whole or part, you may rescind within 72 hours of the denial notice and recover your deposit.
  • Deposits held in trust. Payments must be held in trust until materials are delivered to the site or a substantial portion of the work is complete. A large deposit for a job that will not start for weeks should be questioned.
  • No deductible games. Under C.R.S. 6-22-105 a roofer may not pay, waive, rebate, or absorb your insurance deductible. A contractor who offers to is committing insurance fraud and asking you to join in. We never do, and any estimate that hints at it should be discarded.

A reasonable payment schedule is no deposit or a modest one before materials are ordered, a draw at material delivery, and the balance on completion and final inspection. The statute's required statements should appear in the contract itself. If they do not, the contract may be unenforceable, and you are dealing with someone who has not read the law.

sections.h2: Warranty lines
sections.html:
Two warranties should appear, separately.

  • Manufacturer material warranty, with its term and whether it is a standard limited warranty or an enhanced system warranty that requires the contractor to be credentialed and the full accessory system to be installed. Enhanced warranties often add non-prorated coverage and workmanship coverage, and they have registration deadlines.
  • Contractor workmanship warranty, with its term in years, what it covers (leaks caused by installation), what it excludes (storm damage, foot traffic by others), and whether it transfers to a buyer.

A workmanship warranty is only as good as the company's ability to answer the phone in year six. Ask how long they have been operating under the current name and whether the warranty is in writing. Our warranty page lays out what to ask for on any system.

sections.h2: Red flags and a comparison checklist
sections.html:
Red flags:

  • No measured square count, or a count that differs sharply from other bids without explanation.
  • No line for ice barrier, starter, drip edge, or disposal.
  • "Flashing as needed" or "reuse existing flashing."
  • A shingle described by warranty term only, with no product name.
  • No permit line, or a suggestion to skip it.
  • A deposit larger than the materials, due before anything is ordered.
  • Any mention of covering, waiving, or helping with the deductible.
  • Pressure to sign today, or an assignment of benefits that hands your claim to the contractor.

To compare bids, put them side by side and check that each has the same square count, the same number of tear-off layers, the same ice barrier coverage, the same named shingle and rating, the same ventilation, new flashing throughout, a decking unit price, permit and disposal, and both warranties. Only then compare the totals. The cheapest complete bid is a bargain. The cheapest incomplete bid is a change order with a signature line.

If you want a baseline to compare against, our free inspection comes with a written, itemized estimate that includes every line above.

faq.q: What is a square in a roofing estimate?
faq.a: A square is 100 square feet of roof surface, and it is the unit roofing is priced by. A 2,000 square foot house has more roof than floor because of pitch and overhangs, often 24 to 30 squares. The estimate should show the measured area and its source, and apply a waste factor of roughly 10 to 15 percent to field shingles depending on how cut up the roof is.

faq.q: What does O&P mean on a roofing estimate?
faq.a: O&P is overhead and profit, usually shown on insurance estimates as 10 percent plus 10 percent, applied when a job involves multiple trades or complexity that warrants general contractor coordination. On a retail roofing estimate, overhead and profit are typically built into the unit prices instead. Both are legitimate; the thing to confirm is that you are not being charged both ways.

faq.q: How much deposit can a roofer ask for in Colorado?
faq.a: Colorado law does not set a dollar cap, but it requires the contractor to state its deposit policy in the contract and to hold your payments in trust until materials are delivered or a substantial portion of the work is done. You also have 72 hours after signing to cancel for a full refund. A deposit well above the material cost, due weeks before work starts, deserves questions.

faq.q: Can I cancel a roofing contract in Colorado?
faq.a: Yes. State law gives you 72 hours after signing to rescind and receive your deposit back. If the work is to be paid by an insurance claim and the carrier denies the claim in whole or part, you have another 72-hour window after that denial to cancel. The contract must tell you both rights in writing; if it does not, it may not be enforceable.

faq.q: Why is one roofing estimate so much cheaper than the others?
faq.a: Usually because it leaves something out: fewer squares measured, one tear-off layer assumed, no ice barrier beyond the minimum, reused flashing, no decking allowance, no permit, or a shingle without an impact rating. Line the bids up item by item before comparing totals. The missing items reappear as change orders once the old roof is off and you have no leverage.

h1: Signs You Need a Roof Inspection Before Selling Your Home
title: Roof Inspection Before Selling
description: Signs you need a roof inspection before selling your Colorado home, what the disclosure asks, and how roof age affects insurance. Get a free inspection.
keywords: selling a house with an old roof colorado
excerpt: The roof is the most expensive item on a buyer’s inspection report and the first thing their insurer asks about. Here is how to find out what yours will say before a buyer does.
intro:
In a Colorado home sale, the roof shows up three times: on the Seller's Property Disclosure you sign before listing, on the buyer's inspection report during the objection period, and on the buyer's insurance application before closing. A roof problem discovered at step two or three costs more than the same problem handled at step one, because by then you are negotiating under a deadline with someone who has leverage.

This guide covers the signs that your roof needs a professional look before the sign goes in the yard, what the disclosure form asks, how the contract's inspection deadlines work, why insurability has become the quiet deal-killer on older roofs, and how to decide between repairing, replacing, and crediting.

sections.h2: Why the roof decides so many Colorado deals
sections.html:
Three things make the roof different from every other line on an inspection report.

  • It is the biggest number. A roof replacement on a typical Front Range home is a five-figure item. Buyers who will shrug at a furnace will not shrug at a roof.
  • Hail makes it a known risk. Larimer and Weld counties see hail of one inch or larger most years. Every buyer's agent in Fort Collins or Greeley has seen a deal collapse over an unreported hail claim, so they look hard.
  • Insurers now underwrite the roof. Many Colorado carriers decline to write a new policy on a composition roof past 15 to 20 years, or require an inspection first, or write it on an actual cash value basis. A buyer who cannot bind insurance cannot close a financed purchase.

None of that is a reason to panic. It is a reason to know what your roof will say before anyone else reads it.

sections.h2: Signs you need an inspection before listing
sections.html:
Schedule a professional roof inspection before listing if any of these apply. Two or more and it is not optional.

  1. The roof is 12 years old or older, or you do not know the age. Pull the permit history from the city or county; most keep re-roof permits online.
  2. A hail storm of one inch or larger has hit your area since the roof was installed. Hail bruising is invisible from the ground and obvious to an inspector, and the buyer's inspector will find it. Our guide on spotting hail damage shows what they look for.
  3. You filed an insurance claim on the roof, whether it was paid or not. Claims stay on the property's loss history for years and the buyer's carrier will see it.
  4. You see granules in the gutters, bald spots, curling, or lifted tabs from the ground.
  5. There is a stain on any ceiling, even an old one you painted over. Buyers' inspectors carry moisture meters.
  6. The attic shows daylight, rusty nail tips, or dark sheathing.
  7. There are two layers of shingles. The IRC allows two maximum; a buyer's inspector will flag it and an appraiser may too.
  8. Flashing is rusted, sealant is cracked, or a pipe boot is split. These are cheap to fix now and look like neglect on a report.
  9. The roof has had repairs by more than one contractor, or repairs you did yourself.
  10. Your own insurer has sent a notice about roof age, an inspection requirement, or a change to actual cash value.

A pre-listing inspection is inexpensive relative to the stakes, and ours is free, written, and photographed, which gives you something to hand to a buyer rather than something to argue about.

sections.h2: What the Seller’s Property Disclosure asks about the roof
sections.html:
Colorado's Real Estate Commission-approved residential Seller's Property Disclosure has a roof section near the top. The current form asks you to state, from your actual knowledge:

  • The roof's age and material.
  • Whether the roof is under warranty, when the warranty expires, and whether it transfers to a buyer.
  • Whether roof work was done while a warranty was in effect, and when.
  • Roof leaks.
  • Damage to the roof.
  • Damage to skylights, gutters, or downspouts.
  • Any other roof problem, issue, or concern.

Elsewhere, the form asks whether any property insurance claim was submitted, paid or not, and whether you have written roofing reports or investigations, which you must provide if you have them.

Three points about how the form works. First, it asks for your current actual knowledge; you have no duty to investigate, and you are not expected to know what you have not seen. Second, you must disclose any adverse material fact you actually know, whether or not a box asks about it, and failing to do so can create liability after closing. Third, if you learn something new after signing, you have to update the buyer in writing. A pre-listing inspection converts "I don't know" into accurate answers, and an inspection report you disclose up front is far better than one a buyer discovers you had.

sections.h2: How the buyer’s inspection timeline works
sections.html:
The Colorado Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate sets a series of dated deadlines negotiated into each contract. The ones that matter for the roof:

  • Inspection Objection Deadline. By this date, typically 7 to 10 days after the contract is signed, the buyer delivers a written notice listing unsatisfactory conditions and what they want done: repairs, a price reduction, or a credit.
  • Inspection Termination Deadline. By this date the buyer may simply terminate and recover earnest money if the inspection is unsatisfactory, without negotiating.
  • Inspection Resolution Deadline. If the buyer objects, the parties must sign a written resolution by this date or the contract terminates.
  • Property Insurance Termination Deadline. The buyer may terminate if they cannot obtain acceptable property insurance by this date. This is the one roof age has made important.

The exact dates are whatever your contract says; there is no statewide default, and time is of the essence. A roof objection landing at day eight gives you a few days to get a contractor on the roof, get a bid, and negotiate, with the buyer holding the termination option. That is the worst possible time to learn your roof needs work. Knowing in advance means you can price it in, fix it, or disclose it and let buyers bid accordingly.

sections.h2: Insurability: the quiet deal killer on older roofs
sections.html:
A financed buyer must bind homeowners insurance before closing. Colorado carriers have paid out heavily on hail in most recent years and have responded by underwriting the roof:

  • Some decline to write new policies on composition roofs older than 15 to 20 years, period.
  • Some require a roof inspection or an aerial imagery review before binding, and decline on visible wear.
  • Some will write the policy but only with an actual cash value roof endorsement, which pays a depreciated amount after a hail loss. On a 15-year-old shingle roof that can be a fraction of replacement cost. Many buyers' lenders and many buyers will not accept that.
  • Prior paid claims on the property remain visible in loss history databases for years.

In practice this means a 17-year-old shingle roof can pass a home inspection and still kill the deal at the insurance deadline. Metal, tile, and Class 4 impact-resistant roofs are treated far more generously, and a documented new Class 4 roof usually earns a premium credit that you can advertise. If your roof is in the danger zone, ask your own agent what a new buyer would face, and read our guide to insurance and roof replacement in Colorado.

sections.h2: Appraisal and lender issues
sections.html:
Appraisers note roof condition, and government-backed loans have explicit standards. FHA guidance requires the roof to have a remaining physical life of at least two years, to keep moisture out, and to have no more than three layers; if the appraiser sees damage or cannot observe the roof because of snow, the appraisal is conditioned on a roof inspection before closing. VA appraisals apply similar minimum property requirements. Conventional appraisals are less prescriptive but an appraiser who notes "roof at end of life" invites the lender to require repair or an escrow holdback.

Selling in winter adds a wrinkle: a snow-covered roof cannot be inspected, and an FHA or VA buyer may need a clear-roof inspection or an escrow before the lender will fund. A pre-listing inspection report with photographs from a dry day, kept in the disclosure packet, solves that problem before it arises.

sections.h2: Pre-listing inspection versus a roof certification letter
sections.html:
Two documents help, and they are not the same thing.

A pre-listing roof inspection is a written, photo-documented condition report: material, age, remaining service life estimate, hail or wind damage, flashing and penetration condition, ventilation, and recommended repairs with costs. It tells you what a buyer's inspector will say and lets you decide what to do about it. It is also a disclosure document, so expect to provide it.

A roof certification is a contractor's letter stating that the roof is free of defects and is expected to remain watertight for a stated period, commonly two to five years, often issued after required repairs are completed. Lenders and some insurers ask for it on older roofs. It typically costs a modest fee and is only as good as the company behind it, so it should come from a licensed, insured local roofer who will still be in business when a buyer calls in year three.

Get the inspection first. If the roof is sound or becomes sound after repairs, the certification is a cheap add-on that reassures buyers, appraisers, and carriers at once. Our roof inspection service produces both.

sections.h2: Fix, replace, or credit: a decision framework
sections.html:
Roof situationUsual best moveWhy
Under 12 years, minor flashing and boot issuesRepair before listingCheap, removes report items, keeps the roof off the negotiation table
Hail damage, roof under 15 years, claim not yet filedInspect, consider a claim, replace before listingInsurance may fund it; a new Class 4 roof becomes a selling point and resets insurability
15 to 20 years, no damage, soundInspect, certify, disclose, price accordinglyBuyers can insure with documentation; replacing may not return its cost
Past 20 years, worn, or two layersReplace, or credit at full replacement costInsurability and appraisal will force it anyway; a credit avoids delay but buyers discount it
Active leak or structural issueRepair or replace before listingMust be disclosed; unresolved it invites termination

Two notes on credits. Buyers usually ask for more than the repair costs, because they are pricing in hassle and uncertainty. And a credit does not fix the insurance problem; the buyer still has to bind a policy on the old roof before closing. For that reason, sellers with a roof past 20 years often come out ahead replacing it, especially when financing lets the cost ride to closing. Whatever you choose, make the decision with a report in hand rather than at day eight of an objection period.

faq.q: Do I have to disclose roof problems when selling a house in Colorado?
faq.a: Yes. The Seller’s Property Disclosure asks about roof age, material, warranty, leaks, damage, and other concerns, plus any insurance claims and written roof reports. You answer from actual knowledge, with no duty to investigate, but you must disclose any adverse material fact you know of, whether or not a box asks about it, and update the buyer if you learn something new.

faq.q: Should I replace my roof before selling?
faq.a: It depends on age and condition. A sound roof under 15 years rarely needs replacing. A roof past 20 years, with hail damage, or with two layers often should be replaced, because insurability and appraisal will force the issue and buyers discount credits heavily. A pre-listing inspection gives you the facts and costs to decide, and a new Class 4 roof can be marketed as a benefit.

faq.q: Will a buyer be able to get insurance on my old roof?
faq.a: Possibly not. Many Colorado carriers decline new policies on composition roofs older than 15 to 20 years, require an inspection first, or offer only actual cash value coverage on the roof. A buyer who cannot bind acceptable insurance can terminate under the contract’s property insurance deadline. A current inspection report and certification letter help, and a newer or impact-resistant roof helps more.

faq.q: What is a roof certification letter and do I need one?
faq.a: A roof certification is a licensed roofer’s written statement that the roof is free of defects and should stay watertight for a stated period, commonly two to five years, usually issued after any needed repairs. Lenders and insurers sometimes require it on older roofs. It is inexpensive and reassures buyers, but it should follow a real inspection and come from a local company that will still answer the phone.

faq.q: How long does a buyer have to object to the roof in Colorado?
faq.a: Whatever the contract says. The Colorado contract sets negotiated Inspection Objection, Termination, and Resolution deadlines, often 7 to 10 days after signing for the objection, and a separate property insurance deadline. If the buyer objects, the parties must resolve it in writing by the resolution deadline or the contract ends. Knowing your roof’s condition before listing keeps you from negotiating under that clock.
